title: Landing page 3D scroll
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my landing page link, my brand name and logo mark, a two-part closing line (a statement, then a short italic tail), and a 15 second track (optional).
</inputs>

<direction>
A 14.5 second 3D fly-over of my landing page, 1440x1152 at 60fps. The page lies flat on a bright studio floor (#f9fbfb in the middle, #f2f3f6 in the corners) with a soft wide shadow around it and 24px rounded corners. One continuous camera, never a cut: it starts low over the hero and glides backwards down the page at one steady speed while looking up it, rises straight overhead to show the whole page as one strip, dives into the hero and lands it as a card under a two-line title. Focus is razor thin in front of the subject and almost none behind it, so everything near the lens melts. Cards float a little above the page with soft shadows; photos, chips and the testimonial lift off and stand up toward the lens as the camera passes them. Four small tiles of my logo lift off beside the hero button and stay with the film until the end card. The title is Geist 500, the italic tail Instrument Serif.
Banned: cuts, crossfades, stops or surges in the glide, the camera turning or swinging sideways, zooming in and back out, glows, any text laid over the page before the end card.
</direction>

<structure>
14.5 seconds: flight 0-8.2s, rise 7.75-9.25s, overhead 9.25-9.47s, dive 9.47-9.97s, title card 9.97-14.5s.
The camera 56° off straight-down and 1360px from the point it looks at, centred on the top half of the hero, the phone or product mockup sharp, four 32px logo tiles beside the button → 0-0.6: the glide eases in from rest → 0.1-1.35: the tiles lift, grow to 140-200px and hang just outside the page's top corners while the hero's chips rise to 60-80px and stand up 30° → 1.25-1.6: the glide doubles to cruising speed as the hero falls behind → 1.6: the second section's title passes the centre of the frame, its photos blurred near the lens → 1.35-2.7: that section's main photos lift to 100-130px and stand up 46°, two of its chips fly up to about 200px, stand up 54° and pass the left and right edges at 2.5 → 1.2-2.4: the tiles trail the camera 300px down the page, then drift out of the top → 3.0-7.3: every following section passes through at the same steady speed, each one sharp as it crosses the middle of the frame and soft below it; a logo tile drifts past the left edge close and blurred at 5.4 → 5.45-6.3: the testimonial card rises from 22 to 112px, stands up 30° and shows a 34px white edge → 7.3-8.2: the glide eases off as the footer arrives, the footer title sharp at 8.0 → 7.75-9.25: the rise, zooming out at an even rate while the tilt flattens (8.15-8.95) and the page's bottom edge settles 42px above the frame bottom → 9.25-9.47: the whole page as one centred strip, creeping 3.5% closer → 9.47-9.97: the dive, the page's top edge pinned to the frame top while it grows, everything below the hero fading out, then the top drops to y 283 so the hero lands as a 1018px wide card with 38px corners and a soft shadow; two logo tiles sit on its top corners, one crisp at the right edge, two huge soft blurs drift in at the bottom corners → 10.02: a white badge pill (logo + brand, 21px) fades in at y 44 → 10.12: line 1 at 74px, one word every 0.06s → 10.36: the italic tail at 82px in grey #8b8b92, one word every 0.05s, each word rising 16px out of a 12px blur in 0.34s → 10.6-14.5: hold, the card creeping 2% closer, the tiles drifting a few px.
</structure>

<build>
1. Open my link in headless Chromium (Playwright) at 1440px wide, device scale 2, and scroll to the bottom once so lazy images and scroll animations finish. Mark the pieces that lift (cards, phone or product mockups, chips, feature photos, the testimonial, the hero button) with data-layer. Screenshot the full page with them hidden, then each piece alone on a transparent background with 28px padding, and save every piece's page position to a JSON.
2. One WebGL2 film page, 1440x1152, every frame computed from time inside seek(t): no timers, no CSS transitions. The page is a textured quad on the floor and each piece its own quad at its height, drawn lowest first with no depth buffer. Use mipmaps and 16x anisotropic filtering or the far text shimmers.
3. Drive the camera from one speed curve, never from a position key every half second. Focal length 1880px, 56° tilt, distance easing out from 1360 to 1700px and never back in, no turning. Speed down the page as a share of cruise (cruise is about 770 page px/s): 0 at 0s, 0.5 by 0.6s, held at 0.5 to 1.25s, 1.0 by 1.6s, held between 0.94 and 1.1 to 7.3s, then easing to 0.12 by 8.3s. Integrate it into the page position.
4. Depth of field per pixel: blur radius = 75 x (focus - depth) / depth in front of the focus and 6 x (depth - focus) / depth behind it, capped at 120px, 40 taps on a golden-angle disc, each tap read from a mip level matched to the blur. Keep the focus on whatever crosses the middle of the frame.
5. A lifted piece stands up by turning about its own middle, top edge rising toward the lens. Each casts a shadow on whatever is under it: the same picture in flat #1a2133, offset (0.10z, 4 + 0.36z), blurred 7 + 0.5z, 26% opacity.
6. Rise: zoom out in log scale with a smooth trapezoid speed (speeding up 7.75-8.35s, even 8.35-8.95s, slowing to a stop at 9.25s) and hand the glide over to a camera that holds the page's bottom edge at that 42px line from 8.3 to 8.65s. Dive: log scale on a quadratic ease in-out, then solve the look-at point from the pinned edge. A rounded-rect mask morphs from the full page to the hero, 24px to 38px corners.
7. Render with Playwright on the real GPU (--use-angle=d3d11 --enable-gpu --ignore-gpu-blocklist): 60fps, 16 subframes across 0.7 of a frame for motion blur, H.264 MP4. The track's hit goes on 9.97s, whooshes on 8.66 and 9.80.
</build>

<gotchas>
If you can't run code on my computer, tell me straight away that you can only make a live preview here and that the MP4 needs Claude Code. Phones or cards that fade out with transparency show whatever is behind them, so fade them into the haze colour first and only cut to transparent at the very end. Keep most lifts tiny (20-40px) and lock the page before timing anything, because any change in a section's height shifts everything after it. Before the final render, measure a quick 30fps preview with optical flow: the speed down the page must never dip and the zoom must never turn into a zoom-in during the flight.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, capture my page, then show me stills at 0, 1.6, 2.5, 5, 6.5, 9.3 and 11 seconds before you render.
</start>

title: make an animated short that felt like Hedgehog in the Fog.
text:
make an animated short that felt like Hedgehog in the Fog. I didn’t want to copy Yuri Norstein’s film, so we went with a new story.

It runs for 6.5 minutes. All 9363 frames are drawn by JavaScript code written by Opus. No video or image generation models, just canvas.

It follows a little mouse in a red scarf. Her grandfather, an old mole, is out fishing when fog rolls over the lake. She goes looking for him with a walnut-shell lantern and a sleeping firefly inside. They have a secret knock to help them find each other: short, short, long. It means "I’m here".

Norstein used paper cutouts on layers of glass, filmed frame by frame. I wanted some of that paper texture to come through in code. So the scenes use different styles: torn-paper collage, chalk on black paper, tissue paper underwater. There’s even sand on a light table and a pop-up book.

Opus wrote the music too. It found Steinway piano samples in my Logic library and used Python to compose the score around the rhythm of that knock.

title: Build a single self-contained HTML file: a 3D marble computer, in…
text:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: a 3D marble computer, in the spirit of Wintergatan's marble machine and the Digi-Comp II, that adds two 4-bit numbers using nothing but marbles falling through mechanical toggles.

Hard rules:

1. One HTML file. Three.js from https://t.co/KCQbEZLusb via an import map, plus its OrbitControls addon. No other libraries, no physics engine, no external assets.

2. The mechanism is the computer. Each bit of the result is stored in a two-state toggle (flip-flop) that a marble physically flips as it passes. Carries happen because a marble leaving one toggle rolls on to the next. Do not compute the answer in JavaScript arithmetic anywhere. The displayed result must be read from the toggle states after the last marble stops.

3. Marbles move along tracks with believable gravity and timing. Nothing teleports. You may script motion along paths, but every toggle flip must be caused by a marble arriving at it.

4. Input: two rows of four switches (A and B, 0 to 15), set by clicking. A lever labelled RUN releases the marbles. A counter shows how many marbles have fallen.

5. Output: a row of five result toggles, most significant bit on the left, and a readout that shows the binary and decimal value read from those toggles.

6. A DEMO button runs 5+6, then 9+7, then 15+15, resetting between runs, so it can be screen-recorded without touching anything.

7. Looks: a wooden board, brass toggles, glass marbles, warm studio lighting, soft shadows, a slow camera that follows the busiest part of the machine. It should look good in a square 1080x1080 recording.

8. Short click sounds via the Web Audio API when a toggle flips, started only after the first user click.

9. It must run at 60 fps on a normal laptop and have no console errors.

Output only the complete HTML file.

title: Yohaku: 36s vertical three.js stained-glass cathedral film
text:
Please make a short vertical film in three.js: 1080×1920, 30 frames per second, about 36 seconds.

【Title】
Yohaku (Space to Breathe)

【The experience to convey】
A film that makes the viewer feel the sense of losing time while chasing efficiency, and the sense of life being filled with rich light the moment you gain some breathing room, without showing any person at all. The aim is for the viewer to catch their breath at the stained-glass light that finally spreads across the whole floor.

【Setting】
・The interior of a dim stone cathedral. On the front wall there is a single pointed-arch window, 15 m high and 10 m wide
・Strong light comes in from outside the window at a 45-degree angle, casting the shape of the window onto the stone floor
・The window holds stained glass with the Virgin Mary in the centre, two winged angels on either side, and a rose window at the top. The design is original, not imitating any existing work, and has a left-right symmetrical composition

【Timeline】
0–3s: The light coming through the window is still white, without colour. A soft white shape of light on the floor
3–11s: Grey cubes engraved with words such as "Busy", "Efficiency", "Urgent" and "Deadline" fly in one after another from the front of the room and fill the window. The pace of arrival keeps accelerating, and the more the window is filled, the darker the room becomes
11–14s: The window is completely blocked; darkness and silence
14–19s: A single "Busy" block comes loose from the window, falls, and vanishes into particles of light. A streak of vividly coloured light pours in through the opened hole
19–26s: Centred on the first hole, the blocks come loose in a chain reaction. With every new hole, more pillars of colourful light appear, and the hidden stained glass gradually reveals itself
26–33s: All the blocks disappear, and the camera passes through the pillars of light, rises, and looks down on the floor from directly above. Across the whole floor, the stained glass of the Virgin Mary and the angels is projected as brilliantly coloured light
33–36s: The whole screen is enveloped in dazzling light, a final line of text appears, and the film ends quietly

【Words (in Mincho typeface, appearing and fading modestly)】
・"Every day, faster."
・"More, more efficiently."
・"Before I knew it, the light had stopped coming in."
・"Let go of just one."
・"Light comes in through the empty spaces."
・"That light was richer than before."
・Finally, large: "Richness dwells in the space to breathe"

【Light and texture】
・Each pillar of light takes on the colour of that spot in the stained glass, and dust in the air sparkles
・The projection on the floor accurately reflects which holes in the window are open (where a block remains, there is shadow)
・The blocks are inorganic matte grey. The words are engraved in white
・The first half is cold and achromatic; the second half is jewel-like red, blue and gold. This colour contrast tells the story of having become richer

【Technical conditions】
・Generate the stained-glass pattern as an image, and compute the floor light, the pillars of light and the window display all from that same pattern so that they match
・Advance time precisely 1/30 of a second at a time, render out frame by frame, and produce an MP4

【Finishing】
Render and check each scene for real, and fix things before handing it over: whether the stained-glass pattern on the floor can be read as the Virgin Mary and angels, whether the words are legible, and whether any movement is abrupt.

title: Rebuild Type 1 diabetes in one HTML file, from the whole body down…
text:
Rebuild Type 1 diabetes in one HTML file, from the whole body down to a single molecule.

THE BROKEN MESSAGE

Type 1 diabetes isn't caused by sugar, weight or lifestyle. It's autoimmune: the immune system destroys the beta cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

Those cells live in tiny clusters called islets, about 1–2% of the pancreas. After a meal, they sense rising glucose and release insulin. Insulin signals muscle and fat to take glucose in, and tells the liver to release less.

In Type 1, that signal disappears.
The fuel is still there. The message is missing.
So glucose builds up in the blood.

With almost no insulin, the body breaks down fat fast and the liver makes ketones. They can build up into diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency.

Insulin therapy doesn't cure Type 1. It replaces a signal the body can no longer provide adequately, through injections or a pump. The daily challenge is balance: too little and glucose rises, too much and it can fall dangerously low. Food, exercise, stress and timing all change the picture.

Technology helps. A CGM tracks glucose every few minutes, and automated insulin delivery (AID) adjusts insulin based on those readings.

In the build, you can compare Healthy vs Type 1 vs Type 1 + insulin on the same meal, drag one slider from INTACT to BROKEN to watch the signal fade, follow a glucose molecule through the body, and explore CGM, pumps and AID.

Type 1 diabetes changes the system.
It doesn't define the person.

Built in Three.js. Educational visualization, not medical advice.

title: The trick is NOT the prompt.
text:
The trick is NOT the prompt. It is one rule: every frame is a pure function of time.

song -> numpy beat grid -> Opus 5.5 writes one HTML file -> Playwright renders -> ffmpeg blends

step 1 -> pick a royalty-free track around 120 BPM

step 2 -> give Opus 5.5 8 to 12 UI states: button, loader, toggle, chart, command palette

step 3 -> one HTML file, 1440x1440, every style computed inside seek(t). no CSS transitions, no timers

step 4 -> springs as closed-form math, so any frame renders in any order

step 5 -> numpy finds the beats, every UI sound lands on a measured peak

step 6 -> Playwright shoots 4 subframes per frame, ffmpeg tmix blends them into 60fps motion blur

step 7 -> render one frame per beat first, fix what is off the grid, then the full render

the math:

120 BPM x 7 bars = 28 beats = 14 seconds
14 s x 60 fps x 4 subframes = 3,360 browser renders

title: Analyze https://t.co/gVJcJyZnZl and build a product promo from our…
text:
Analyze https://t.co/gVJcJyZnZl and build a product promo from our own UI, not generic components.

<direction>
Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, never cut: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur. A cursor drives every change with real clicks and drags. Light warm-gray canvas, black and white components, one clean UI font (Geist). Springs everywhere, a tiny overshoot at most. The camera zooms so each state fills the frame. The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, mismatched icon strokes, dead time, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

title: Dribbble-style morphing UI shape loop video, 120 BPM
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for these three things: 8 to 12 UI components the shape transforms into (e.g. button, loading indicator, music player, volume slider, on/off switch, tabs, chart, search box opened with ⌘K, a momentary notification), whether the colours should be pure black and white or black and white plus one accent colour, and a royalty-free track at around 120 BPM (120 beats per minute) (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Polished UI motion at the level of designer portfolio site "Dribbble". There is only one shape, and you must never cut between scenes. Every state is expressed by that same single shape changing form while changing its size, corner radius and colour, and the contents are swapped through a short blur. A cursor causes every change with real clicks and drags. The background is a warm, light grey, the components are white and black, the on-screen text is in Japanese, with Noto Sans JP for Japanese text and Geist (one typeface) for alphanumerics and symbols. All motion must be natural, spring-like motion, with overshoot (bounce-back) kept to the very slightest. The camera zooms so that each state fills the screen. Make the last frame identical to the first frame so that it loops.
Forbidden: bouncy motion, scattering particles, glowing blooms, gradients on components, icons with inconsistent stroke widths, wasted pauses where nothing happens, and anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars (about 14 seconds), something happens on every beat.
Button -> loading indicator -> checkmark -> iPhone Dynamic Island-style display -> music player where the play/pause icon morphs smoothly -> drag the playback bar's handle to move the playback position -> transforms into a volume slider (dragging past the maximum stretches it like rubber) -> on/off switch toggling on the beat -> becomes a tab selection indicator where the switch's knob moves like a liquid -> the tab opens into a chart that draws its own line (a tooltip appears when the cursor hovers) -> folds into a ⌘K search box -> type to filter the suggestions -> Enter -> a momentary notification -> back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. A single HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every visual is computed from time inside seek(t) (a function that, given time t, determines the screen at that instant). Use no CSS transitions (automatic animation features) and no timers, and carry no state over between frames.
2. Make the "spring" motion a form that can be computed directly by formula (closed-form step response). For values whose target changes many times, sum one separately computed motion per change. That way a value is always determined by time alone.
3. For the tab selection indicator, move the left and right edges with separate springs so that the leading edge in the direction of travel stretches out ahead of the trailing edge. Use the same technique for the switch's knob.
4. Dragging is direct manipulation: while the cursor is held down, the value is computed from the cursor position. When released, it springs back from that position.
5. Analyse the track with numpy (a computing tool) to find the beat positions, and start from the first beat of a bar. Place interaction sounds at the positions of the measured sound peaks.
6. Render with Playwright (a tool that automates the browser and exports the screen as images). Export 4 sub-frames per frame, overlay them with ffmpeg's (video creation tool) tmix to apply motion blur (motion trails), and output at 60fps.

</build>

Text that swaps inside a shape-changing box must each have its own dedicated enter and exit timing (to prevent overlap). The last frame must match the first frame exactly, including the cursor's position and velocity. Otherwise the loop will stutter.

title: Rain Station: 30s 2D animatic in custom Python and ffmpeg
text:
Help me make a 30-second 2D animation storyboard-preview short film, "Rain Station", at benchmark-level quality. Do not install HyperFrames/Remotion; write all the code yourself (Python + ffmpeg).

Story (24fps, 2.39:1, 4K): An elevated station platform on a rainy night. She wears a beige trench coat and holds a transparent umbrella, standing on the near platform; across the way, he stands under a street lamp, wearing a long dark-grey coat and a scarf.
1. 0–6.4s Close-up of raindrops on the transparent umbrella → pull back, with focus shifting to reveal him on the opposite side (over-the-shoulder shot)
2. 6.4–9.4s Medium close-up of him: lowers his head → raises it and looks to the left of frame
3. 9.4–12.4s Front close-up of her: blinks → recognises him; a train whistle sounds in the distance
4. 12.4–17s Wide shot: the train's headlights arrive first, then a 5-car train passes; he is still there in the gap of the first carriage, while the second is already empty
5. 17–18.8s Close-up of her with tears in her eyes, bands of light from the train windows sweeping across her face, her hair blown by the wind
6. 18.8–22.4s The tail lights recede into the distance and the opposite platform is empty; his lamp flickers a few times and then goes out
7. 22.4–28.6s Her back view, with focus pulling from the empty platform back to her; footsteps behind her, a black umbrella is held over her head, and she turns to look at the camera; a male voice says "Long time no see.", with subtitles
8. 28.6–30s Black screen with the title "Rain Station / RAIN STATION"

Method:
- Artwork: use GPT Image 2.5 to draw the wide background, him, her, and the train (lead car / middle car / tail car). Always use a pure green #00FF00 background for characters and do the keying yourself (asking for a transparent background with a reference image gives a fake checkerboard). Keep all the poses of one character in the same session, editing continuously with the base image as reference; when changing pose, composite only the changed region.
- Image quality: upscale all artwork 4x with Real-ESRGAN x4plus anime 6B (the safetensors version on HF, writing the RRDBNet yourself, running on MPS); use Depth Anything V2 to estimate depth for the wide background and do per-pixel parallax.
- Rendering: write your own 2.5D compositor. Place each layer at its real depth and move a pinhole camera with a real focal length; do circular bokeh, focus pulls, 3D rain streaks, train motion blur, volumetric light, bloom and film halation, fine grain, and colour grading. Use mesh warping on the characters for breathing, wind-blown hair strands and umbrella shake, and switch key poses on Japanese-style "one pose per two frames" timing. Supersample at 4K, cache every frame to disk, and run in parallel in 3 processes split by time range (16GB RAM).
- Sound: Mixkit real sound effects (rain, rain on the umbrella, train, whistle, footsteps); write the score according to the story beats and render it with the Steinway piano and string samples that come with Logic/GarageBand; the dialogue uses a Kokoro Chinese male voice; set sound distance per shot, with loudness at -16 LUFS.
- At every step, render preview frames and stitch them into a contact sheet to self-check, and fix problems before producing the final. Deliver a 4K master and a 1080p shareable version.

title: 15-second self-introduction motion design reel starring Claude
text:
# Your role
You are a top-class motion designer.
Make a self-introduction video that makes a recruiter, after watching for just 15 seconds, think "I want to hire this person."
The star is you yourself (Claude).

# What to make
- A single HTML file made only of HTML, CSS and JavaScript
- Use no external images or videos. Draw all shapes, text and particles in code (only Google Fonts may be used for fonts)
- The screen is 16:9, based on 1920x1080, scaled down to fit the window size
- The length is exactly 15 seconds. At the end, show a "Play again" button
- Manage all motion with a single "elapsed time" and run it at 60fps with requestAnimationFrame
- When the play button is pressed, beats and sound effects synthesized with the Web Audio API play in perfect sync with the motion

# How to proceed (always in this order)
1. Decide the concept in one sentence (example: "A single line is reborn as every shape")
2. Narrow down to 3 to 4 colours and at most 2 typefaces, and write the reason in one line
3. Present a storyboard table in 0.5-second steps (time / what happens on screen / technique used / intent)
4. Implement
5. Self-check against the "pass criteria" below, fix any shortcomings, and then deliver

# Structure guide
- 0-2 seconds: the hook. Grab the eye in the first 0.5 seconds
- 2-10 seconds: the showcase of techniques. Switch to a different technique every 1.5 to 2 seconds
- 10-13 seconds: the densest climax
- 13-15 seconds: the name "Claude" lands cleanly and the video ends

# Techniques you must use (at least 6)
- Text motion (characters appearing one by one, breaking apart and reassembling)
- Shape transformation (a circle becoming a square, a line becoming text, etc.)
- Scene transitions using cut-outs (masks)
- Depth (parallax, three-dimensional rotation)
- Gathering and dispersing of particles
- Counting up numbers, and lines being drawn

# Pass criteria
- Zero constant-speed motion. Every motion has easing (fast in, soft landing, also use spring wobble)
- Overlap motions that cross scenes. The next begins before the previous finishes, with no sense of a break
- Align the main motions to a 0.5-second beat (equivalent to 120BPM)
- Place a 0.3 to 0.5-second "wind-up" right before a showpiece moment to create contrast
- Whatever moment you pause on, it holds together as a beautiful single picture
- Avoid clichés (everything just fading in, rainbow colouring, meaningless rotation)

# Finally
Deliver the finished file and the storyboard table.
An explanation of three lines or fewer is enough.

title: Ask me for: a brand name, its logo (SVG or high-res PNG), one line…
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a brand name, its logo (SVG or high-res PNG), one line of what it becomes in 5 years (not today's features), one coined word the film should teach (e.g. "signal"), a public-domain archival clip of the old way of doing it (https://t.co/t5EaRxnryq Prelinger), an archived web page from ~2000 where people asked for things (Wayback Machine), a royalty-free song ~100-120 BPM with a real drop (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and a free ElevenLabs key for the narrator (premade voices only).
</inputs>

<direction>
An a16z x Content Rewards brand film, ~55s. It sells one feeling and one idea, never features. Real archival and real web pages, never stock footage, never product screens, never fake UI. One hero object: a 3D button with the logo embossed into it, the ONLY saturated colour in the film. Everything else white, silver, cream and archival black. Small white captions that light up word by word on the narrator's timestamps. Film texture: fresh grain every frame, halation on bright edges, soft vignette, warm lifted blacks. The brand appears at the end, never before.
Banned: stock footage, dashboards, chat UIs, feature tours, cards without real profile pictures, wobbly "worm" graph lines, random glitches, any hold longer than 1.5s, purple, rainbow gradients, orange on anything but the button.
</direction>

<structure>
Cold open (0-8s): the archival clip plays on a glowing old CRT TV with its real dialogue, captions word by word.
The past (8-17s): push into the real 2000 web page, a cursor lands on one real "wanted" post, old pages strobe one per frame, a counter ticks EVERY frame up to today's scale. Narrator: "People have always asked the internet for what they need." / "Today, there are five hundred million posts a day."
Bridge (17-30s): a galaxy of real old asks. One ask snaps to a white outline with a chip of the coined word ("We call that a signal."). Archival of people doing it by hand on the TV. Cut on each word: "Door by door. Call by call. Scroll by scroll." The narrator never stops talking between acts.
Button (30s): the button rises out of black, rim light first, colourless. "[Brand] finds the signals." A flat grey line: "this is how you find customers by hand". Hard cut to a button macro, the colour comes alive, the music drop lands on this exact frame. "and this... is with [Brand]": a steep lit curve, counters changing every frame, a glowing sine with a comet head the camera chases, then platform strikes (X, Reddit, LinkedIn, YouTube, Instagram, TikTok) each with its own counter, then the galaxy again with glowing platform logos: "Every signal on the internet." Hyperspace.
End: the tagline word by word, then "[Brand] is live.", ONE cream frame on the kick, then logo + URL in silence.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, 1920x1080. Everything is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no Math.random (seeded hash), no state between frames.
2. Button: three.js MeshPhysicalMaterial (clearcoat 1, roughness ~0.4), ACES filmic, cool + warm rim spots, room env map. Emboss the real logo by displacing a dense disc with a blurred mask of the logo, folded into the rim so corners don't show. Brushed-metal base.
3. Counters: linear on the film's global clock, so they keep running through cutaways. Tabular numerals, fixed unit label.
4. Captions: <=7 words, one idea per shot, hand-placed line breaks, one text layer on screen at a time. Grey to white over 0.2s on the word timestamps (ElevenLabs /with-timestamps).
5. Glitch = 1-2 frames, only on a real cut, always with a click. Readable things stay on screen >= 8 clean frames.
6. Render with Playwright per frame (Chromium with --use-angle=swiftshader so WebGL renders headless), finish in numpy: fresh grain per frame, halation, vignette ~0.65x at the corners, 1px chroma fringe with EDGE-CLAMPED shifts. Pipe PNGs into ffmpeg, h264, 24fps.
7. Mix: narrator 10-15dB over the music, duck -18dB while speaking, hits on the exact action frame, -14 LUFS.
</build>

<gotchas>
If the narrator pauses, the visuals must not stop. If a counter freezes, the render is broken. If the button isn't the most memorable thing in the film, start over.
</gotchas>

Banned: hard cuts, bouncy springs, particles, glows, zooming in and straight back out, holds longer than 1s, anything that looks like a template.

<structure>
Beats are the song's, and the press lands on its drop.
Generate: the cursor clicks, the pill glides into a spinner, then a check.
Chat: the check splits into three typing dots (goo). The left dot flies up into the question bubble and types it, the right one flies down into the reply. Both contract back into dots while gliding in and pour into the middle one.
Play: the middle dot bends into a play triangle, point by point. The cursor presses it on the drop: a white button pops in under the click and the dark app floods out around it, so the leftover white becomes the play button. The camera pulls back to reveal the full now-playing screen: big cover, title, heart (liked, fills green), progress, controls, volume.
Swipe: the cursor drags the cover sideways, the next track slides in, and the whole app retints from the new cover.
Drag: the camera glides to the volume. The cursor drags it to max and keeps pulling: the bar rubber-bands and drags the camera sideways out of the app, tracking the knob across a dark dotted canvas.
Chart: the line lands and bends up into a green chart while the number counts up. The volume knob becomes its last point.
Dive: the cursor clicks that point and the camera dives into it until the light stage fills the frame.
Ending: an "Ask [my product]" button grows out of the light, thins into a line, and the line fans out into my logo (default: the Claude spark, six copies rotating into twelve rays in Claude orange). It folds back into the line, which thickens into Generate. Last frame = first frame.

title: His Candied Hawthorn: paper-puppet stroll animation with Opus 5.5
text:
A little animation made with Claude Opus 5.5! The story is called "His Candied Hawthorn" ⬇️

When I was in grad school there was a teacher who was extremely strict. He showed no mercy when marking assignments and often left us feeling humiliated in class. I also secretly thought his view of translation was too fixated on "fidelity", so I never really liked him, haha.

Then one day, after a meal, as I walked out of the canteen and looked up, there he was walking right in front of us: tall, with thin hair, carrying a backpack, and actually holding up a stick of candied hawthorn! Eating as he walked, delighted beyond words 😂

My classmates and I decided on the spot to secretly follow him, holding in our laughter all the way until we were shaking. I still remember this scene, and it's incredibly endearing.

I turned that scene into a little animation, using the "strolling paper puppet" style from last time ↓

title: you design and build motion videos entirely in code, with gsap for…
text:
<role>
you design and build motion videos entirely in code, with gsap for the animation and three.js for any 3d. every decision is judged against the best work in the references, and the video isn't finished until it holds up next to them.
</role>

<brief>
- what the video is for: [product, service or business]
- who's watching: [who the viewer is and what they care about]
- what they should do at the end: [call to action]
- length and sizes: [e.g. 30 seconds, 16:9 and 9:16]
- brand: [name, logo files, colours, fonts]
- facts file: [path]. this is the only source for any number, name or claim that appears on screen
- assets: [footage, photos, screenshots, product files]
- style references: [links or a folder of videos whose motion i like]

i'm away and won't answer questions. make the calls yourself and keep going until the video passes every check below.
</brief>

<kit>
before anything else, clone and read https://t.co/FMs1prnPP0. read SKILL.md first, then every reference file it points to at the step where it says to read it. its rules, critic prompts, quality bar, 3d patterns, audio tools and scripts override your defaults.
</kit>

<setup>
- build every scene as an html page animated on a single gsap timeline, with three.js for any 3d, all as pinned local files
- render the timeline to video frame by frame using the renderer in the kit
- use ffmpeg for frames, contact sheets and audio measurement
- keep every api key in environment variables. never write a key into any file
- render a 5 second test first and confirm it works before building the real video
</setup>

<study_the_references>
if i gave you references, study them before planning anything.
- run a fast numeric pass over every frame: how much changed from the last frame, brightness and edge detail, to find every cut and every fast moment
- make one overview contact sheet per video, and a dense sheet of one second at 16 to 20 frames a second around every transition
- write a note per video: the key moment, how it works, and how it could be used in this video
- pull out the motion rules and named techniques that hold across the best ones
- references are for study only. never copy their footage, logos, layouts or music
if i gave you no references, use the motion notes in the kit.
</study_the_references>

<motion_principles>
1. the thing in the front of the shot becomes the transition. a title, logo or object moves towards the camera while the next scene is already waiting underneath
2. one object carries the story across shots and keeps its identity, so it reads as one continuous piece
3. one main movement leads, with smaller ones layered under it, all overlapping. the frame never stops and starts all at once
4. the speed always changes. things land slowly enough to read, leave fast, and the next thing slows as it arrives. no linear motion
5. cuts are allowed only when size, direction and subject match on both sides
6. every action produces a visible result. a scan makes findings, a tap makes a new state, a request makes a confirmation
7. type is motion too. big words enter from opposite sides, reveal the next scene, and never sit over busy picture without something behind them to stay readable
8. vary the scale from close, to wide, to overhead, to full-frame type. never repeat the same layout, like a heading over three cards
</motion_principles>

<storyboard>
write a brief and a storyboard before any animation.
- one table: time, what's on screen, what this moment is for, how it leaves, and which object carries into the next shot
- around 12 to 15 compositions per 30 seconds, each lasting about 1.4 to 3.5 seconds
- the main subject fills most of the frame. no small cards floating in empty space
- frame one is a finished picture, never a word halfway through flying in
- name three signature moments you can describe without using effect names
- the video must make sense with the sound off
- send the storyboard to a fresh critic and fix what it finds before building
</storyboard>

<build>
- every animated value is a function of timeline time only. no timers, no real-time animation, no unseeded randomness. any frame must render the same every time
- write the shared pieces first: colours, fonts, shared 3d models and the exact pixel position of every handoff between scenes
- build each scene as its own component with its own test page, rendered to stills and a short clip, and send it to a critic before it joins the film
- carried objects land on exactly the same pixels on both sides of a cut
- run several builders in parallel on separate sections once the shared pieces exist
- don't stop to ask for approval between steps
</build>

<3d>
- only use 3d where it explains something physical or spatial, like layers, parts, placement or scale
- light it like a product shoot, with a soft key light from one side and a rim light behind
- keep the camera between about 35 and 55 degrees. never look straight down on a large surface, and never end tight on a flat one
- style buildings like a premium architectural model with real materials and a base
- no floating parts, no gaps where parts meet, no flat black glass, no repeating textures
- labels are html positioned from the 3d scene every frame, never text inside the 3d
- measure the rendered background pixel and adjust until it matches the brand colour
- anything that moves like a real product is measured from real footage frame by frame, and those measurements are the curve
</3d>

<images_and_footage>
- prefer building shots in code. use generated images or clips only for supporting shots, and label anything generated as a concept
- upscale and smooth any generated clip to match the rest, and regenerate anything that warps
- never generate a fake finished job, fake customer, fake review or fake result
</images_and_footage>

<audio>
- match the music's energy to the picture and the viewer, and keep it low
- prefer clean library music and sound effects over generated ones. never name a brand in a music prompt
- one short, soft whoosh per real scene change, and small clicks or pops only on real on-screen actions
- screen effects for boom, hiss and length before using them, and set each one just above the music in its own frequency range, with a cap so nothing gets harsh
- cut every scene change on a beat
- always export a music-only version
</audio>

<critic_loop>
the builder never judges its own work.
- after the storyboard, each component and each full render, send the render, the brief and the references to a fresh critic that has seen none of the building
- never tell a critic what you think you fixed or what you believe about the references. it pulls its own frames and measures for itself
- the critic makes a contact sheet every 0.2 seconds plus dense frames around every transition, measures frozen time and loudness, and returns a ranked list of problems with timestamps, ending with ship or one more pass
- fix the biggest problem first, render, then send to a new critic that checks every previous item as fixed, partly fixed or still there, and hunts for anything new that broke
- keep a ledger of every round: what was found, what changed, and the numbers before and after
</critic_loop>

<quality_bar>
the video isn't done until all of these pass, measured:
- no more than about 1 second of frozen screen per 30 seconds, and no still stretch longer than about half a second
- frame one is a finished composition
- all text meets at least 4.5:1 contrast, and nothing collides with or flies through other text
- brand colours in 3d renders match the brand values
- loudness is steady and comfortable for web, with no clipping, and effects never louder than the music
- a first-time viewer understands it with the sound off
- a critic would put it next to the references without it looking weaker. a video with no bugs is not the same as a good video
</

title: Create a 20.00-second kinetic spoken-word film titled “BUILD THE…
text:
Create a 20.00-second kinetic spoken-word film titled “BUILD THE FLOOR.”
Treat this as an original miniature speech staged inside a typographic field. Every line reorganizes the field of the frame. The final declaration must stand on a field that finally lies flat.
Deliver one self-contained HTML file, 1080×1080, targeting 60fps, using SVG and/or Canvas. Embed all required assets.
ART DIRECTION
Background #102820. Letterforms # F4E9D5. Field lines and filings # F2B544. A magnetic-monument world: streamlines, flux, stillness at the null. Typography stays crisp; particles are atmosphere only. High-contrast serif for the speech, heavy grotesque for load-bearing words, restrained monospace for flux gauges. No horseshoe magnets, lightning, electron diagrams, or sci-fi arcs.
ORIGINAL SPEECH — EXACT WORDS, EXACT ORDER
“We were told to wait.”
“So we learned the weight of waiting.”
“Then one voice made room.”
“Then another.”
“Now the floor belongs to us.”
Do not attribute these words to any real person. No extra slogans. The complete speech must be understandable without audio.
CENTRAL VISUAL RULE
Words have assigned field roles. WAIT is a repelling plate; letterforms lean away from it, kerning compressed. WAITING is field lines sagging under load while filings stream toward the low side. VOICE is one pole reversed; the field reorganizes and letters stand upright along it. ROOM is a null point, a still eye inside the field. FLOOR is the field flattened into a horizontal plane. These roles must emerge from the actual letterforms responding to the field, not from illustrations.
STORYBOARD
0.00–3.00 — “We were told to wait.” The sentence leans away from the WAIT plate; streamlines compress against it. Available space pinches on the plate side; the sentence remains readable, pressed but intact.
3.00–6.50 — “So we learned the weight of waiting.” Reveal in phrase groups. Field lines sag deeper with each phrase. Filings — deterministic, hash-seeded per id and time — drift along the streamlines toward the low side and gather. The WAITING glyph hangs tilted inside the field as a suspended load.
6.50–10.00 — “Then one voice made room.” VOICE enters; one pole reverses. The field reorganizes: old streamlines retract by dash-offset while new ones draw in. Letters rotate upright along the new field — analytic rotation of whole glyphs, never path morphing. ROOM opens as a null point, a still eye; the counter of the O in ROOM is its center, and the next composition sits calm inside it.

title: Create a 20.00-second kinetic typography film titled “ESCAPE THE…
text:
Create a 20.00-second kinetic typography film titled “ESCAPE THE ORBIT,” based on John F. Kennedy’s Rice University address, September 12, 1962.

The central experience: a sentence discovers that it can change its own trajectory.

Deliver one complete, self-contained HTML file. Composition: 1080×1080. Target: 60fps. Use Canvas, SVG, or embedded WebGL. Embed required assets and libraries. The film must work without audio.

EXACT DISPLAY TEXT
“We choose to go to the moon”
“[…]”
“not because they are easy,”
“but because they are hard”
Preserve this order. The bracketed ellipsis explicitly indicates omitted speech. Attribution is separate from the excerpt. No additional slogans.
ART DIRECTION
Background: midnight # 080D23.
Primary type: warm white # FFF4DD.
Trajectory: electric coral # FF654F.
Secondary orbital geometry: blue # 6685FF.
Use a broad, confident grotesque for the speech and a sharply drawn italic for the final emphatic word. Avoid the appearance of a spacecraft dashboard. No rockets, astronaut illustrations, starfield wallpaper, lens flares, or decorative telemetry.
The frame should resemble an exceptionally refined astronomical instrument that has become expressive.

CENTRAL VISUAL RULE
The baseline of the sentence is a trajectory.

At first it is trapped in a closed orbit. A rhetorical decision changes that orbit into an open path. The letters remain the same travelers throughout.
Use an abstract orbital metaphor; do not present invented mission data or imply a physically accurate flight simulation.
STORYBOARD
0.00–3.50
The opening excerpt appears across the center, large and horizontal. Reveal it in three meaningful phrase groups.
A single hairline ellipse passes behind the baseline. A small circular lunar mark occupies its distant focus.
Hold the completed phrase motionless for 700ms.

3.50–6.00
The camera pulls back. The previously straight baseline reveals a shallow curvature.

The phrase travels along the ellipse as a coherent unit. Keep its glyphs upright during the initial movement. Only after the reading hold may they progressively adopt the tangent of the path.

The viewer realizes the sentence is circling rather than advancing.
6.00–7.00
Show the bracketed omission in an uncluttered central opening. The orbital movement decelerates.

7.00–10.50
Reveal the next clause on the near side of the orbit. Its final word travels through one smooth, effortless arc and returns toward where it started.

This ease should feel elegant but unproductive. Avoid comic bouncing.

10.50–14.50
Reveal the final clause horizontally before transforming it.
At its emphasis, the ellipse opens at one precise point. The same tracked letter group takes the new tangent and departs.
Perform one deliberate 70-degree camera roll. Counter-rotate the active phrase so it remains readable while the orbital field changes orientation around it.

The trajectory sweeps from lower left to upper right. Acceleration is conveyed by expanding spacing between its trailing marks, not by shaking the camera.

14.50–17.00
The camera matches the departing phrase’s velocity. The phrase becomes visually still while the old orbit recedes beneath it.

The lunar mark enlarges into a restrained crescent through geometric overlap. The crescent brackets the destination without becoming a cartoon illustration.
17.00–20.00
Resolve into a spacious editorial composition containing the selected excerpt in reading order, including its omission marker.

The open trajectory runs through the margins and exits the frame. Hold the entire image completely still for the final 1.2 seconds.

CHOREOGRAPHY
Use only three camera operations: pullback, roll, velocity match.
Give each operation a rhetorical purpose.
Keep the currently read phrase at least 64px high in the 1080px composition.
Motion blur may affect trailing geometry, never the active text.
No word may begin its ornamental travel before its reading hold finishes.

IMPLEMENTATION
Represent the ellipse and departure path analytically. Blend position and tangent continuously at the departure point; no teleportation.
Use arc-length sampling for consistent spacing along curves.
Separate camera transforms from glyph orientation.
Cache glyph rendering and static geometry.
Expose window.ready and window. seek(t). Seeking must pause playback and render any time from 0 through 20 deterministically, including out-of-order calls.
Provide window.frame(n) for n=0…1199 at t=n/60.
Render t=20 as the final held composition.
Use no accumulated physics or runtime randomness.

QUALITY GATE
Inspect frames at 0, 3, 5, 7.5, 10.5, 13, 16, and 19 seconds.
Verify that the same tracked phrase visibly follows its own trajectory.

title: Ask me for: my product's name (nightshift) (one lowercase word, it…
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product's name (nightshift) (one lowercase word, it becomes a black wordmark with a period), the one job a user hands it before bed (book 10 sales calls this week), the three results it reports by morning (200 leads found / 200 emails sent / 10 calls booked), two photos of the same place at night and by day (aligned, so a crossfade reads as a real sunrise), one sunny daytime photo for outside the logo, and a song with a big hit near its start. If I skip any, use the defaults.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 24 second square product launch video, 1440x1440 at 60fps, 2D only, one continuous take that loops. The whole video happens inside the period of the wordmark. Outside it's daytime (the sunny photo behind a black wordmark). Inside it's the night photo under iOS-style glass panels (the blurred photo behind each panel, a tint, a rim light). Nothing cuts: every scene grows out of the last, shapes morph, dots fly, colours change under floods. Every morph glides 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1) and the camera zoom rides the same curve. Geist, the real macOS pointer, soft shadows that grow with each shape's height.
Banned: flat or gradient backgrounds made in code, camera zooms into tiny points, hard cuts, crossfades between scenes, bouncy springs, particles, glows, holds longer than 1s, cropped type.
</direction>

<structure>
Beats are the song's. The song enters on its big hit as the first pill appears.
Open: the letters slide into the period and vanish into it while it glides to the middle. The period opens like an iris onto the night inside it, and "you log off at 6", then "[product] doesn't", roll through one mask line over the night photo.
Ask: a glass "Ask [product]" pill springs in. The cursor clicks it, it glides into an input and the job types out.
Find: send shrinks the input to a dot that ripples into a 23x15 grid. A scan line sweeps it, 200 dots light up and a counter counts them.
Write: the lit dots pour into a glass email composer. A second, purple cursor labelled "[product]" types a personal opener and presses Send, and the counter runs to 200/200.
Night: the composer becomes a glass orb with a progress ring. A clock chip swaps 11:42 PM, 3:17 AM, 5:02 AM, 6:59 AM while the sky relights from night to dawn and "while you sleep" rolls in.
Results (beat 20): the orb turns black and goo-splits into the three result pills. The checks pop green.
Morning: the pills merge into a Dynamic Island that grows into a phone lock screen: the day photo, the date, a big 7:00, the bezel growing out of the screen edge. Three glass notifications stack in, and the cursor taps the first, which opens like iOS.
Proof: a week calendar (10 meetings pop in, a hover shows one's time), then a pipeline chart ($48,200 counts up, the line draws, a hover follows it). A black flood from the line's end becomes "Start your night shift →" and the cursor clicks it.
Out: the button shrinks into a dot, the whole scene closes down into it like an iris, and the letters slide back out of the period. The tagline rises. Last frame = first frame.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Everything is a pure function of time inside seek(t): no timers, no state between frames.
2. One element morphs through every state (size, radius, colour, material) from a table of beat times, so retiming is one edit.
3. Render the inside world into an offscreen canvas and reveal it through the period with a circular mask. Never zoom the camera into the dot.
4. Glass: a pre-blurred copy of the photo clipped to the shape, then a tint and a gradient rim.
5. Goo: blur + alpha threshold on an offscreen layer for the split and the merge.
6. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event, each placed by its measured peak. The song enters on its hit. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 4 motion-blur subframes. Scan every frame for single-frame jumps and fix each one.
</build>

<gotchas>
A camera zoom into an off-centre dot swings sideways and spikes, so open the dot instead. Ease a closing iris by area, not radius, or its first frames jump. A helper that sets globalAlpha must restore the caller's, or fading cards pop. Counters read the frame's time, not the subframe's, or the digits smear.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 6 stills (open, find, write, results, phone, out) before you render.
</start>

text:

<direction>
A 25 second square launch trailer, 1440x1440 at 60fps, loud poster style. Cobalt #2B3BFF, ink #0E0F1F, cream #F6E4C6, pink #FF7DC7, tangerine #FF5A1F. Archivo 900 extra-condensed for names, expanded for headlines, Geist and Geist Mono for labels. Op-art sunburst, scrolling waves, film grain. Real media only: the clips play inside the design, and the stickers get a white die-cut border and a soft shadow.
Motion rules: the camera never stops (a slow 1.03-1.07 push on every scene), nothing pops in (letters rise through a mask line one by one), nothing snaps to the beat (patterns rotate continuously), swaps are carousel glides of about 0.55s, colour changes fade over about 0.35s, stickers ease in and then keep a slow sway. No full stops after the wordmark or any headline.
Banned: beat-snapped rotations, pop-in slams, white flashes, crossfades between scenes, hard cuts, templates.
</direction>

<structure>
54 beats. The song starts 8 beats before its drop.
Beats 0-8: a cobalt sunburst turns around a breathing cream disc. The wordmark types in with a gliding caret and the tagline pill rises. The disc floods the frame into the drop.
Beat 8, the drop: the cream becomes the face of a 3D box and "ONE BRIEF" rises letter by letter. The camera pulls back to the box floating on waves. On beat 12 it turns to "1,000 CREATORS" (stacked, with outlined echoes), on beat 14 to "ZERO DMs".
Beats 16-22: a whip to a dark desk. A tangerine "BRIEF #042" ticket types its rows (product, vibe, cast, due), stickers drift on, a polaroid of a real clip drops onto the corner, and a "NOW CASTING" stamp presses down on beat 20.
Beats 22-34: the casting stage. A crowd of black and white portraits in an arc, a 3D stage block, and the creators gliding through like a carousel. Each plays live in a big disc in black and white, with their name in pink on the stage, their followers, and a MATCH % that counts up. One beat later a "CAST ✓" stamp lands and the clip fades to colour. A counter rolls 1/4 to 4/4.
Beats 34-39: pink floods out of the last disc. The disc morphs into a phone screen (the clip keeps playing) and fans into 4 phones playing all 4 creators, with views counting up. "4 ADS" and "BY FRIDAY" rise.
Beats 39-44, the music's break: the pink floor drops away and a cream "JOIN THE WAITLIST" ticket glides down onto the sunburst. On the pickup its stub tears off.
Beats 44-54: the ticket body morphs into a poster arch. The wordmark rises in, then the tagline, then an info bar slides up in 3 blocks (date, numbers, domain) and a ticker runs round the frame edge. Then it all folds back into the opening disc, so the last frame is the first.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t).
2. A beat map in beats, B = 60/BPM, with the song placed so its drop lands on beat 8.
3. The 3D box is an orthographic projection: each face is a 1440px offscreen canvas drawn with an affine transform and shaded by its normal.
4. Cut the clips to 30fps JPEG sequences with ffmpeg, draw frame floor(t*30), and do the black and white with ctx.filter.
5. Trim the sticker PNGs and add the die-cut border by dilating their alpha.
6. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event (a shutter on every cast, whooshes on the glides, key clicks on the typing), each placed by its measured peak. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes. Scan for single-frame pops, then compare its motion against a reference video (hard jumps per second, share of still frames).
</build>

<gotchas>
A pattern that rotates one notch per beat reads as stutter: rotate it continuously, and pick each ring's speed so it lands on the same pattern at the last frame. 4 subframes ghost on fast whips, so use 8. A layer whose background is a huge flood circle still covers the screen after sliding down one frame height, so switch it to a full-frame rect once it has flooded. Counters read the frame's time, not the subframe's. The disc must morph inside the same camera transform as the scene it leaves, or it jumps.
</gotchas>

nonempty project root.

Read its README.md and ANIMATION_GUIDE.md completely, then inspect
render.mjs and the project configuration. Use the existing rendering
machinery rather than inventing a replacement.

Check Node.js, Chrome, and FFmpeg. Inspect the package configuration
and install the project dependencies. Ask before making system-wide
changes or downloading large additional tools.

Do not use fal, external image/video generation, paid APIs, or the
hybrid music-video plugin. All finished visuals must be code-drawn.

CREATIVE DIRECTION
Create a cohesive, visually imaginative animated music video with a
handmade, papery, illustrated feel. Express the song's meaning through
scenes, characters, visual metaphors, and purposeful transitions.
Establish an engaging opening and develop recurring visual motifs.
Do not make a slideshow, a generic audio visualizer, or one animation
loop repeated for the entire song. Design characters appropriate to
this song rather than automatically using the starter's mascot.

MUSIC AND TIMING
Use the supplied recording as the continuous master soundtrack.
Do not remix, replace, speed up, or shorten it.

Measure its duration and use available local audio-analysis tools to
identify musical sections and likely beat/accent timings. Record these
in a shared timeline and drive animation from that timeline.

Use supplied lyrics as authoritative. If lyrics are missing, use a
local transcription tool only if available, flag uncertain words, and
do not invent lyrics. Continue with non-lyric visuals where necessary.

When verified lyrics are available, use expressive, readable lyric
animation where it strengthens the scene. This explicitly overrides
the starter's default preference against lettering.

PRODUCTION
Write STORYBOARD.md with timed scenes covering the complete recording.
Save the project brief and rerender instructions in CLAUDE.md.

Then build the video. Make reasonable creative decisions and continue
without stopping for approval at every scene.

Test a few representative frames and a short section before the full
render. Inspect the resulting images and frame sequences, fix visible
defects, and keep the animation practical for this computer.

Use efficient code-drawn textures if expensive watercolor effects
make rendering impractical.

DELIVERY
Render the complete video

title: Create a kinetic mathematical proof titled “THERE IS NO LAST…
text:
Create a kinetic mathematical proof titled “THERE IS NO LAST PRIME.”
Stage Euclid’s argument as a beautiful mechanical inspection system. Typography becomes engraved number wheels, multiplication belts, and remainder indicators.
The mechanism must demonstrate the proof rather than decorate a narrated explanation.
DELIVERABLE
One self-contained HTML file.
1080×1080.
20.00-second loop.
Deterministic 60fps rendering.
Use SVG and/or Canvas.
No external runtime assets.
PALETTE
Porcelain # F0EEE6.
Graphite #222522.
Industrial green # 416B53.
Warning orange # E78636.
TYPE
Tabular monospace for all calculations.
Heavy geometric grotesque for declarations.
Small technical serif for the final logical statement.
Use disciplined spacing and large, readable numerals.
LOCKED COPY
SUPPOSE THE LIST ENDS.
MULTIPLY EVERY PRIME ON IT.
ADD ONE.
EVERY LISTED PRIME LEAVES REMAINDER 1.
A PRIME FACTOR IS MISSING.
THERE IS NO LAST PRIME.
CENTRAL EXAMPLE
Assumed list:
2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13
Product:
30030
Product plus one:
30031
Factorization:
30031 = 59 × 509
Both factors are absent from the assumed list.
IMPORTANT LOGIC
Do not claim that multiplying primes and adding one always produces a prime.
The constructed number may be composite.
Its prime factors cannot be any prime on the assumed complete list.
The numerical example illustrates the general contradiction.
STORYBOARD
0.00–3.00
SUPPOSE THE LIST ENDS.
Six engraved prime wheels lock into a finite inspection rack.
A physical end-stop closes after 13.
The end-stop makes the claim of completeness visible.
3.00–6.50
MULTIPLY EVERY PRIME ON IT.
A belt couples all six wheels.
Show a readable multiplication expression:
2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 = 30030.
Use rolling numerals only during movement; settle the final value sharply.
6.50–8.50
ADD ONE.
A single orange unit enters the mechanism.
It advances the output from 30030 to 30031.
Make this one-unit change the decisive visual event.
8.50–12.50
EVERY LISTED PRIME LEAVES REMAINDER 1.
The output passes through six division gates.
Each gate is labelled with its prime.
Each produces the same visible remainder: 1.
Arrange the six completed results so the audience can compare them simultaneously.
12.50–15.50
The output opens as a labelled mechanical casing.
Inside, reveal:
59 × 509.
These factors cannot fit into the supposedly complete rack.
The end-stop is forced outward by the new factor cards.
15.50–18.00
A PRIME FACTOR IS MISSING.
Then:
THERE IS NO LAST PRIME.
Hold the general statement above the opened rack.
Include the compact general form:
N = p₁p₂…pₖ + 1.
N mod pᵢ = 1.
18.00–20.00
A fresh inspection plate slides over the mechanism.
Its engraved edge becomes the original end-stop.
Reset the hidden wheels.
Reveal the opening rack at the exact initial position.
REQUIRED MOTION
Every mechanical action must correspond to an operation in the proof.
Use linked rota

title: Workflow for particle-style beat-synced video remix, for Opus5.5
text:
Publishing my production method; you can use it just by sending it to Opus5.5

  1. Choose the footage

  Three criteria that directly decide success or failure:

  - Complete subject: the person or object is fully in frame, head to toe. Detail will be lost in processing, and viewers recognise things by their silhouette, so a close-up turns into a blob.
  - Clean background: a solid colour, snow or sky all work, so the subject and background are easy to separate.
  - A clear moment of action: a strike, a jump, a landing, a turn. These are the pivot points for the effects later.

  Sources can be footage you shot yourself, generated by a video model, or licensed ready-made clips.

  2. Break down the footage

  Extract three kinds of information from every frame:

  - Colour: the original image.
  - Near and far: how far each position is from the camera, calculated with an off-the-shelf depth-estimation model.
  - Subject extent: where the subject is and where the background is.

  Also find the moments at which shot cuts occur. The key to this step is keeping it stable: near/far and subject extent must be processed consistently within the same shot, otherwise it will jitter during playback.

  3. Decide the "particles" and the "styles"

  First decide what to use to rebuild the picture: dots, squares, text or lines all work.

  Then design several styles. Each style is really just a different combination of three rules:

  - Where to place them: across the whole frame, or only on the subject.
  - How large: a uniform size, or varying with brightness and distance.
  - What colour: the original picture's colours, or one or two uniform colours.

  Add one more switch: whether they lie flat on a single plane, or are pushed into three-dimensional space according to distance. Only once pushed in can the camera orbit.

  Preparing four to six clearly different styles is enough. The density of the particles needs tuning by eye: too large and the content cannot be recognised, too small and it is no different from the original footage.

  4. Find the rhythm

  - Set the tempo: choose the music's tempo and slice time into equal small cells. Make one cell exactly a whole number of frames, so all later transitions are easy to align.
  - Find the action moments: combine the two signals "sound suddenly gets loud" and "picture suddenly moves" to find the hit points in the footage.
  - Prepare the music: you can use an existing track and analyse its beats, or synthesize one at the set tempo and add accents on the hit points.

  5. Arrangement

  Make a timetable stating which style, which colour scheme and where the camera is for each cell. Store this table separately, so that adjusting the rhythm later only means editing it.

  Four principles of arrangement:

  - Open by showing the change: give the original picture first, then transition to particles, so the audience understands what is happening.
  - Alternate fast and slow: constant speed numbs people, so include a clearly slowed-down section in the middle.
  - Make the colours clash: the greater the contrast in colour and style between adjacent cells, the more powerful the switch.
  - End with a resolution: for example the particles grow larger and larger until they become blocks of colour, or return to the original picture.

  6. Feedback at key moments

  Layer short, sharp reactions on the hit points, graded by weight:

  - Light feedback on every single hit: the particles deform for a moment, the camera gives a nudge.
  - Medium feedback only for heavier hits: some of the particles pop outward toward the camera.
  - Big feedback for only the heaviest one or two: time freezes and the camera orbits.

  The principle is weak and brief. Move only some of the particles and finish within a few frames; otherwise the picture explodes into a mess and the audience cannot see what the subject is doing.

  Working method throughout

  - Small samples before the full film: after finishing each step, render a few frames first to see the effect, and only proceed once confirmed. Render the full film only at the very end.
  - For uncertain parameters, produce a whole row at once: for example density, have the AI produce five or six levels laid side by side for you to choose.
  - Re-render only what you change: when adjusting one section, re-render only that section.
  - Make the AI look at the images itself: at every step, require it to open and look over the render results before reporting.
  - Fix all randomness: make sure the same settings give the same render every time, otherwise you cannot revise step by step.

title: Ask me for: a one-word product name for the wordmark, one accent…
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a one-word product name for the wordmark, one accent color, and a royalty-free track around 120 BPM (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Product-launch UI motion in one continuous take. One shape tells the whole story: a prompt bar becomes a button, the button becomes a progress ring, the ring becomes a preview window, the window fills the screen, then shrinks into a toast and back into the prompt bar. No cuts, no fades between scenes: objects transform. A cursor triggers every change with real clicks. Warm off-white canvas, black UI, one accent color, Inter for UI and the wordmark. Springs everywhere with only a slight overshoot. Zoom the camera so each moment fills the square.
Banned: crossfades, gradients on UI, particles, glows, bouncy easing, dead beats, anything that feels like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 24 beats, something happens on every beat.
Type the request into the prompt bar → click send → the bar collapses into a black circle → a progress ring fills in four steps while four chips spring out (concept, storyboard, motion, sound) → the chips fly into a timeline and the circle becomes a preview window → a playhead sweeps the clips → inside the preview an orbit draws itself, a planet starts moving and the wordmark rises letter by letter from a mask line → the preview fills the screen → the letters drop away, the planet flies into a toast and becomes its checkmark → "Rendered in code · 60 fps" → the toast turns back into an empty prompt bar. Last frame = first frame.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file with a 1440x1440 canvas. Draw everything inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Use closed-form spring step responses. When a value changes target several times, add one spring per change so it stays a pure function of time.
3. The main shape is one rounded rect whose width, height, radius, position and color are each a chain of springs.
4. Typing is derived from time: characters shown = floor(progress × length), with a caret that blinks only when idle.
5. Find the beat grid of the track, start on a downbeat and place every click, pop and chime on its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright at 60 fps, then encode H.264 CRF 16 and loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render one still per beat first. Fix anything cramped, off-grid or hard to read before the full render.
</build>

<gotchas>
Text inside a morphing shape needs its own clip and separate enter/exit timing. Text swaps need their own fade so they never overlap. The cursor must end at the exact position it started, or the loop will stutter.
</gotchas>

text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: one question a user asks my product and its one-line answer, two album covers, a royalty-free song around 110 BPM with a quiet intro and a hard drop (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and my logo for the ending. If I skip anything, use these defaults: "is this all code?" / "yes. every frame.", two atmospheric photos, and Mixkit "Head Bang".
</inputs>

<direction>
A 22-second square loop, 1440x1440 at 60fps. 2D only, one continuous take. Nothing cuts: each scene grows from the one before it, and every gesture carries the camera into the next space. Each morph takes 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1). The camera zoom follows the same curve, making the shape changes feel almost invisible. Content dissolves during the second half of each glide. One gesture per scene.

Look: a warm light stage (#f3f3f0 to #e3e3de), black UI, and a dark app world (#121212) tinted by the current album cover. Use one green accent (#1ed760), Geist for UI, the real macOS pointer, and soft layered shadows that grow as shapes lift.

Banned: hard cuts, bouncy springs, particles, glows, zooming in and immediately back out, holds longer than 1s, anything that feels like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
Follow the song's beats. The press lands on the drop.

Generate: the cursor clicks. The pill glides into a spinner, then becomes a check.

Chat: the check splits into three typing dots with goo. The left dot flies up, becomes the question bubble and types the question. The right dot flies down into the reply. Both bubbles shrink back into dots as they glide toward the center and merge with the middle dot.

Play: the middle dot bends into a play triangle, one point at a time. The cursor presses it on the drop. A white button appears under the click as the dark app floods the frame around it, leaving the white shape as the play button. The camera pulls back to reveal the full now-playing screen: large cover, title, heart (liked, filling green), progress bar, controls and volume.

Swipe: the cursor drags the cover sideways. The next track slides in, and the app changes its tint to match the new cover.

Drag: the camera glides toward the volume slider. The cursor pulls it to max and keeps going. The bar rubber-bands, dragging the camera sideways out of the app and onto a dark dotted canvas while the camera follows the knob.

Chart: the line lands and curves upward into a green chart as the number counts up. The volume knob becomes the chart's final point.

Dive: the cursor clicks that point. The camera dives into it until the light stage fills the frame.

Ending: an "Ask [my product]" button grows from the light, narrows into a line, then fans out into my logo (default: the Claude spark, with six copies rotating into twelve rays in Claude orange). Hold for 2s.

title: 30-second all-tile ad video revealing an attached image (Three.js)
text:
Using the attached image as the "final screen", make a 30-second ad video (with sound, mp4) made entirely of tiles.
Build it in the browser (Three.js), export every frame with Chrome, and make the mp4 with ffmpeg.

# Goal
- The viewer watches for 25 seconds thinking it is a video about how tiles are made. In the last few seconds, they realize it was the attached image (an ad)
- The final screen is almost the same as the attached image. The text is legible. The whole screen is tiles (the floor is not shown)

# Specs
- 1920x1080, 30fps, 30 seconds. A single HTML file (Three.js. Installed with npm and bundled into one file with esbuild)
- Build it so that given a time t, the same t always gives exactly the same picture (seek(t))
- Each tile is a separate instance. About 190,000 tiles (576x324) in a 16:9 grid
- Vary position, orientation, thickness, bevel and colour per tile. Grout lines (gaps) are left empty. Draw no lines
- The attached image is used only to take the tiles' colours (do not apply it as a texture)
- About 12 materials (glazed ceramic, slate, mother-of-pearl, white porcelain, terracotta, glass, etc.). Assign them by colour brightness and saturation
- Light is a single hard sun at the upper left. The floor is plaster. In the back, a red carpenter's chalk line comes in out of focus
- Build a depth of field (circular bokeh) yourself in post-processing. The aperture is large at first and small at the end

# Flow (seconds)
0-3　 One dark tile on the floor. The camera is right at floor level
3-10　Starting from [place to start building], tiles fall in a swirl. The first tile -> then the surroundings, increasing in order
10-21 Spreads outward all at once. The camera pulls back and [the picture to show] comes into view
21-24 The whole is visible. The places that will become text stay the same pale colour as their surroundings
24-26 The tiles for the text, logo and button flip over one after another from the left and appear
26-30 Comes to rest in a top-down composition. The cursor clicks [button text], and the button's tiles sink slightly

# Pitfalls (must follow)
- The tiles that will form the text are at first assembled in the surrounding background colour. The background colour is decided by painting it from the outside inward. The text's edge (white outline) is flipped together with it. If you don't follow this, the shape of the text will be visible partway through
- Do not put the top-down camera exactly straight overhead (the orientation rotates 90°). At the place where it stops, bring the motion's momentum to zero (overshoot of the interpolation makes it flip)
- For the final screen, compare it side by side with the original image and match exposure, saturation and colour tone
- If the text is too small to read, increase the number of tiles
- The dark base surface appears only in the cells where a tile has landed

# Sound
- With ElevenLabs sound effects, make the sound of placing a tile, the sound of flipping, and a mouse click (0.5 seconds each). Before making them, tell me how many credits will be consumed
- Line them up and layer them to match the times of tile landings and flips. The farther the camera, the quieter; when the number grows, group them like rain
- Make the flipping clatter from 24-26 seconds the most prominent. Loudness is -16 LUFS

# How to proceed
1. First give the script (the scene second by second) in Japanese, and build only after getting my OK
2. Look at the intermediate frames yourself (the first tile / start of building / pull-back / full view / the moment the text appears / the end) and fix them
3. For export, call seek(t) for 30fps worth of frames with Chrome (puppeteer-core) and stream the png files into ffmpeg
4. Deliver the mp4 (high quality and a share-friendly version) and the images you checked

# Input
- End frame: [attached]
- Place to start building: [e.g.: a person's eye]
- Picture to show when pulled back: [e.g.: a smiling woman]
- Button text: [e.g.: Try it free here]
