title: No plugins, no app, just a single HTML file running Three.js on…
text:
No plugins, no app, just a single HTML file running Three.js on WebGPU.

It's an interactive 3D house that builds itself in five stages: Foundation → Skeleton → Systems → Envelope → Finished. Every part has its own window on the timeline, so you can scrub through the construction like a video.

What's inside:
→ X-ray mode that makes the structure transparent and shows the water, power, sewage and airflow routes, with filters for each system
→ Explode, to pull the layers apart
→ Cut, a section plane that slices through the building
→ Dusk, a lighting switch to see it at night
→ Instanced vegetation, so a dozen olive trees cost almost nothing to render
→ Callouts and preset cameras for each stage

The subject is a traditional hillside villa, but the format works for any building. A developer could show a buyer exactly what's behind the walls before a single wall exists.

title: Ask me for: a voiceover or song with a spoken line (the audio…
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a voiceover or song with a spoken line (the audio file) and its transcript, 10-12 small objects that sum up my life, two silhouettes to light like a heat camera (a head in profile and a raised hand), and the 3 words I want to land hardest. If I skip any, use the defaults: vinyl, book, camera, cat, coin, game controller, cap, heart, money, plant, clapperboard, skateboard; free CC0 silhouettes from Openverse; action, intention, curiosity.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 20 second 4:3 film, 1440x1080 at 60fps, cut to the voice. Off-white paper, black, one red, one yellow, Geist for every word. Film grain on everything, a soft vignette, and a camera that never rests: a slow handheld float under everything plus a slow push inside every scene.
No scene cuts to the next: each handoff starts on the exact last frame of the scene before. The only hard cuts are the beat flips on the last word.
Every object is pixel art you draw yourself: a 16x16 grid per object, every cell a hand-placed colour, rendered as a 3D block (a darker extrusion down-right, a thin bevel on every cell) with a soft contact shadow.
The silhouettes are lit like a heat camera: the heat comes from how thick the body is at each point, so the nose, the hair and the fingertips run cooler, plus one hotspot and a slow moving noise, mapped through a black > red > orange > cream ramp. The edge stays razor sharp, with a soft glow outside it.
Motion rules: nothing pops in (eased glides of about 0.5s with a soft start), fast moves get real motion blur instead of ghost copies, and captions type with the voice behind a block cursor.
Banned: stock footage, AI video, 3D camera moves, particles, glitch.
</direction>

<structure>
Hang every scene on the transcript's word timings (measure them with faster-whisper word timestamps, one short chunk at a time):
1. The first word fills a yellow card. The card wipes off to the left and the question types underneath on two centred lines that glide to stay centred as they grow, the key word underlined in red as it's spoken.
2. The objects streak past in lanes above and below the words, a cyan four-point flare sweeps in, then the page burns away: black closes in from the edges onto the head, behind a hot red edge.
3. The head heats up on black while the answer types low on the left. A thin white orbit draws itself around the head, its far half passing behind it. On the last word, paper blooms out from inside the head with the objects in it, and the camera falls through: the head rushes past the lens until the paper is all we see.
4. The objects sit on a tilted ring seen in perspective (the front ones bigger and lower, drawn last), slowly turning, each one bobbing; the coin flips and lands with sparks.
5. On each of the 3 words, that object flies out of the ring to the left and grows, the page floods black from it, and the word types beside it (camera: a red shutter star; book: a red ribbon sweep; record: two white orbits and red notes). Then the flood drains back into the object as it flies home, and the camera dives closer into the ring. Put each hero object in the slot that is front-left when its word lands.
6. The ring pulls in a touch, bursts outward, every object turns to ink, and ink blots grow and swallow the page.
7. The hand rises into frame, hot, with the line split either side of it. The heart drops into its palm, then lifts to the centre at the size the next scene holds it.
8. The last word, one letter per beat, the background flipping paper / black / red, the heart holding its place across the cut, the centre object morphing pixel by pixel into the next one.
9. Thin brush strokes sweep through, the letters drift apart and float, then settle back into the word with the heart above it. The camera keeps pushing through the hold.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t).
2. Bake each pixel sprite once to an offscreen canvas (the extrusion layers, then the face), then draw it scaled and rotated.
3. The heat: precompute each silhouette's base heat once (a distance transform of the mask, held at the edge value outside it so nothing dark bleeds in when it is upscaled). Every frame, add the hotspot and two octaves of value noise at quarter resolution, map it through a 256-step lookup, upscale it, and cut it with the full-resolution mask.
4. The fall through the head: draw the ring scene into an offscreen layer, mask it with the head scaled up about a point inside the skull, and grow that scale on a cubed curve until the head covers the frame. The ring inside zooms less than the head does, so it reads as depth.
5. The pixel morph: pair every cell of object A with a cell of object B and glide each one's position and colour, with a small random delay per cell.
6. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes, then lay the original audio back on with ffmpeg.
</build>

<gotchas>
A mask PNG with no alpha channel fills the whole box with heat, so put the silhouette in the alpha. A limb cut by the photo's border shows as a straight edge, so extend the mask past the frame. A handoff only reads as smooth when the last frame of one scene is the first frame of the next: draw the outgoing scene under the transition, and give scenes that show the same ring one shared zoom function. A flood that's still retreating when the next scene starts reads as a hard cut, so let it finish first. A fast ease-out flood reads as a jump; use a soft start.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, measure the word timings, then show me 8 stills before you render.
</start>

title: Picture a butterfly with no memory of its last wingbeat.
text:
Picture a butterfly with no memory of its last wingbeat.
Ask it for frame 720 and you get frame 0, pixel for pixel.

720 frames. 12 seconds. 6 counters. All at 0.

Opus 5.5 can't hand over a video file, one builder says. He made that gap the method.

> STAGE - one fixed 1000x1080 canvas, fonts baked in
> RENDER - a windowless engine calls draw(f) once per frame number
> ENCODE - ffmpeg writes H.264, pixel aspect ratio declared
> CHECK - three passes after every build

By his account the model writes only the first, a drawing program. The other three get reused.

Each picture depends on its number alone: no clock, no timer, no dice that land differently each run.

So any frame renders the same every time. A fix is a small edit and a re-render.

The sample loop is 720 pictures in 12 seconds. A hand animator at 12 drawings a second would need 144.

The smoke test plays one loop unseen and counts six kinds of defect, from script errors to text on text.
Six yes/no gates before a human looks.

The seam check puts frame 0 against frame 720. One changed pixel means some motion isn't periodic.

He reports a last render of 1,820 frames with six zeros. At the sample's 60 fps that would be about half a minute.

Let one frame read a clock and the same number stops giving the same picture.

We drew the rule as an X-ray butterfly, its wingbeat computed from the frame number ↓

title: Build a 30-second looping motion design showreel that introduces…
text:
<direction>
Build a 30-second looping motion design showreel that introduces CLAUDE, a motion designer.
Concept, in one line: one pencil line gets promoted three times (graphite on paper, wire on a blueprint, light on black) and never leaves the screen.

Every shot is made out of the previous one: shapes, type and colour transform into the next scene. No cuts, no fades.

Typeface: Geist only. Weight 900 for big words, 600 to 800 for small labels (24 to 28 px, tracked 0.14 to 0.3 em).
Palette: paper cream #EDE6D5, blueprint blue #1B3ED2, hologram cyan #45F0DD, plus black #07080A, graphite #16161A and white. Each stage's accent is the next stage's colour: blue pencil on paper, cyan on the blueprint, white on the hologram.
Camera: locked and front-on for the whole film, like a drafting table. Objects turn; the camera never moves.
Empty border: nothing at rest within 150 px of the sides or 90 px of the top and bottom. Things travelling through may cross it.

Three inks. The same geometry is drawn in whichever ink is on screen:
- PAPER: a cream paper background (use my paper image if I give one, otherwise flat cream with fine drawn grain) with a 60 px blue grid at about 13% and every fifth line at 26%. Lines are pencil: resampled and pushed off true by slow sine waves whose phase changes 8 times a second, stroked twice (full width at 90%, half width at 40% with more wobble), with paper tooth knocked out of the strokes, then multiplied onto the paper. Fills are diagonal hatching drawn on one line at a time. Big type is hatching cut to the letter shapes, with a doubled outline.
- BLUEPRINT: flat blue with the same grid in white. Clean white lines 3 to 4 px, hidden edges dashed and thinner, fills are fine clean hatching.
- HOLOGRAM: black with the same grid in cyan. Cyan lines with a white core 30% of the line width. Fills are horizontal scan lines on an 8 px pitch whose thickness follows how lit the surface is. No blur halo anywhere: it reads as light through line density only.

Banned: particle bursts, glows, lens flares, camera shake, RGB split, crossfades, generic gradients, bouncy easing, holds longer than half a second, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 60 beats, 15 bars of 2 seconds. Something happens on every beat. Moves start 0.05 s before their beat so they land on it.
Easing: a critically damped spring, 1 - (1 + w t) e^(-w t) with w between 12 and 40, so nothing ever passes its target; exponential ease-in and ease-out for wipes, presses and exits.
Scene changes: paper to blueprint by a shape that floods the frame with a hard edge; blueprint to hologram and hologram to paper by one horizontal scan line.
The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Two corner labels stay on all film: top left "FIG. 07 — GEAR" (bar number and name), bottom right "BEAT 27 / 60". Bar names: DRAFT, TYPE, CURVE, MORPH, TILE, SOLID, GEAR, PANEL, DATA, LIGHT, WAVE, GLOBE, DRUM, FORM, END.
</structure>
<mascot>

The creative director: a small box character. Body 76 x 54 units with rounded corners, two short arm stubs (24 x 16) at mid height, four straight legs (11 x 33), two tall rounded-rectangle eyes (8 x 14). Draw it about 250 px wide. Its right arm is raised 58 degrees holding a pencil.
On paper: graphite outline with sparse blue hatching and graphite eyes. In the hologram: cyan outline with scan-line fill and white eyes. It is never a fourth colour.
It runs with alternate leg pairs lifting, six steps a second, leaning 7 degrees into the run.
</mascot>
<storyboard>

Bar 1, HOOK, 0-2 s, paper.
Frame 0: CLAUDE in Geist 900, fitted to 1500 px wide, centred, pencil-hatched. INTRODUCING small above it, A MOTION DESIGNER small below. A pencil rail 1620 px wide sits 96 px above the letters. The mascot stands on the rail at x = 1560 with CREATIVE DIRECTOR lettered to its left.

0.0: the small lines un-type; the mascot runs off the right edge, accelerating.

0.36 to 0.5: the rail drops, accelerating, to 26 px below the baseline and presses the letters flat into itself.

1.0: the line rises to the middle, shortens to 1320 px and splits into two rails 140 px apart; 41 blue ruler ticks sweep along the top rail.

1.5: the rails open to 300 px; a blue height dimension draws at the right with a live number.

Bar 2, KINETIC TYPE, 2-4 s, paper. Words sit between the rails and are clipped to that slot; the rails move to fit each word.

2.0: INTRODUCING rises through the baseline letter by letter, then lifts out through the top.

2.5: A MOTION whips in from the left (1400 px in 0.2 s).

3.0: the rails clap shut on it and reopen, stretching DESIGNER out of the line; its letters then fly out sideways.

3.5: CLAUDE in blue pencil, letters dropping from above one every 0.05 s. At 4.0 the rails close and crush it into one line 1476 px long.

Bar 3, CURVES, 4-6 s, paper.

4.1: the line gets pen-tool handles (430 px long at 58 degrees, small squares at the ends, circles on the handle tips, the label EASE) and bends into an S.

4.5: the handles swing to the mirror angle; eight blue copies fan out 34 px apart, joined at both ends like a leaf.

5.0: handles retract; the ribbon becomes travelling sine waves (amplitude 92 px, 2.75 cycles, each line a little out of phase).

5.5: it gathers back into one flat line.

Bar 4, SHAPE MORPH, 6-8 s, paper.

6.1: the line curls into a circle of radius 235 (curvature grows, length stays). 6.5: triangle, turning 120 degrees as it changes. 7.0: square. 7.5: hexagon, point up, radius 270. Blue hatching builds inside, then cross-hatching.

Bar 5, TILING, 8-10 s, paper.

8.0: the hexagon shrinks to radius 96 and six more slide out around it. 8.5: twelve more, a honeycomb of

19. 9.0: dense hatching sweeps across until every cell is solid blue. 9.6 to 10.0: the centre cell's shape grows past the frame with a hard edge; inside it is the blueprint, with the honeycomb in white line.

Bar 6, 2D TO 3D, 10-12 s, blueprint.

10.0: three lines draw inside every hexagon, plus three dashed hidden ones: each is a cube seen corner-on. 

10.5: the eighteen outer cubes slide into the centre one, which grows to radius 270. 11.0: it turns a quarter and perspective switches on. 11.5: it faces front.

Bar 7, MECHANISM, 12-14 s, blueprint.

12.0: the cube flattens and its front square grows teeth: a 16-tooth gear, pitch radius 208. title: White ball UI motion loop
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a target value for the slider, three short notification messages, a reply to type, one accent color and a royalty-free track around 120 BPM. If I skip anything, use 100, "Slider - Reached 100", "Gravity - Something is falling", "Messages - What now?", "retry" and electric blue.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 10-second 2D UI motion film in 16:9. Place everything on a near-black canvas with a faint dot grid. Use charcoal controls, sharp white text, one blue accent and a white ball that moves through the entire film. A real cursor makes the opening click feel physical; the ball guides each transition that follows. Keep the UI clean and the impacts precise, with only small spring overshoots. Move the camera through one continuous layout so every interaction fills the frame.

Banned: hard cuts, stock footage, glows, particle bursts, disconnected transitions, excessive bouncing and blurry text during camera moves.
</direction>

<structure>
Around 10 seconds, with something happening on every major beat.

Toggle: the cursor clicks a blue switch. Its white ball springs free, and the camera follows it toward a horizontal slider.

Slider: the ball lands on the knob and moves it along the track. The blue fill stays attached, while a value bubble above the knob climbs to 100.

Notifications: hitting 100 sends the ball onward and brings in three dark cards: "Slider", "Gravity" and "Messages". Each arrives on its own beat. The camera follows the ball down to "What now?".

Reply: the small "Reply" pill stretches into a text field. A keyboard rises below it as part of the same scene.

Keyboard: the ball strikes the keys while "retry" appears in the field. It lands on Return, the blue send button activates and the reply contracts into a small blue message.

Return: the camera pulls back to show the toggle, slider, cards and keyboard together in one world. The ball travels back to the first switch. Match its position, the cursor and the switch state to the opening frame so the film loops cleanly.
</structure>

<build>
1. Make one HTML file at 1920x1080 and 60fps. Calculate every visual from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Arrange all UI components in one world. Use a single camera transform with position and log-space zoom, making each close-up a move through that world.
3. Give the white ball one continuous route between the toggle, slider, cards and keys. Use closed-form springs for landings and a brief squash on impact.
4. Calculate the slider fill and number from the ball's horizontal position. Keep the tooltip centered over the knob until it reaches 100.
5. Give every key press a fixed time. Show the reply as the portion typed by that moment, so any frame can be rendered independently.
6. Align the click, slider movement, card arrivals, key taps, send and return with measured beats. Add a subtle UI sound to each contact.
7. Render one still per beat to check pacing and readability, then export the full film with Playwright at 60fps. Inspect fast camera moves and the loop boundary frame by frame.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never let the ball teleport between components: show the path of every handoff. Keep the value bubble attached to the slider knob. Leave enough space for the notifications to stay readable during camera moves. The keys the ball presses must match the text appearing in the field. Match the first and last frames, including the ball's direction and cursor position, to prevent a loop stutter.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and four stills (toggle, slider, notifications, keyboard) before building the full video.
</start>

title: Food craving launch film
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product, the exact request a user types into it, 6 to 8 photos for the result cards, a royalty-free song around 130 BPM with a clear drop (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and my brand mark for the end card. If I skip anything, use the defaults: the food-ordering story below, food photos from Pexels (fire noodles, birria tacos, hot chicken, buffalo wings, smash burger, spicy ramen), and Mixkit "Cat Walk".
</inputs>

<direction>
A 15-second product launch film, 1920x1080 at 60fps. 2D only, one continuous take. No fades, blurs or cuts: each scene grows from the last. Text rises from a mask line, buttons expand into pages, and color floods from one object before shrinking into another. Give the camera one eased move per scene, and never zoom in and out consecutively.

Look: warm white canvas (#f5f5f2), black UI (#0e0e10), lime accent (#cdf24f), orange (#ff6a2a), and a blue send button (#2f6bff). Add an Apple Intelligence-style iridescent glow around the input: a blurred conic gradient rotating through pink, orange, lime, cyan and violet. Use real food photography on dark cards, Geist for UI and a serif for the product name on the end card.

Banned: crossfades, blur-ins, 3D, particles, camera moves that reverse direction, holds longer than 1s, anything that feels like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
130 BPM, 32 beats (14.8s). Start the song 12 beats before its drop.

Beats 0-6, ask: push slowly into the glowing composer, about 3x zoom. Type the request over three fixed lines with a natural keystroke rhythm:
"I'm really hungry, I don't know
what I want but something
spicy, crispy and filling"

Beat 6, send: press the send button. A lime ripple spreads from it and transforms the message into a chat bubble. Pull back once to reveal the phone around it (428x900 screen, 11px black bezel, 9:41 status bar).

Beats 6-12, think: the send button grows into an orange wok, a half-disc with a thin handle. It tosses 6 colorful ingredients on beats 8, 9, 10 and 11 beneath the shimmering text "Finding something for you…".

Beat 12, the drop: a lime circle expands from the wok to fill the frame in about 0.35s. Dark food cards (330x440, radius 28, photo on top, name, one-line description, price and rating) burst in from the center. Slide the strip across three cards and land on "Fire Noodles", which lifts with a "Best match" pill.

Beats 16-21, chat: the lime contracts back into the user's bubble, carrying its words as the chosen card flies into its slot. "Found it. Fire Noodles from Wok & Fire, smoky, spicy and seriously filling." rises in, followed by "Want me to order it for you?" Then show two pills: "Order now" in black and "More options" outlined. The cursor clicks Order now → spinner → "✓ Ordered".

Beats 21-32, outro: the black button expands into the page, staying pill-shaped as it reaches the edges while the camera pushes into it. Its label grows to headline size, then slides away. Bring in "You were craving noodles." and "Now it's on the way." word by word (92px, white on black). A courier dot follows a route to a pin. The pin becomes the brand mark, and the wordmark wipes out from behind it, with "made with" above and the product name below.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, 1920x1080. Compute every style from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Use one camera transform on a container, keyed by [time, zoom, x, y] with eased segments and zoom interpolated in log space.
3. Use closed-form step-response springs for every pop and settle.
4. Make every handoff a shared element: the lime flood carries a copy of the bubble's words, and the button carries its label into the page.
5. Sound: use a downloaded Mixkit SFX for each event - typing, send pop, each toss, drop impact, card swoosh, click, success tone, page-fill whoosh and mark sparkle. Place each by its measured peak and loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
6. Render with Playwright at 60fps using 8 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix. Review every fast moment frame by frame and scan the full video for single-frame pops.
</build>

<gotchas>
Four subframes leave ghost copies on fast moves, so render 8 and slow the move down. The flood must reach the farthest corner and take about 0.35s, or it looks like a flash. Set z-index on every layer so the cards don't float above the flood. Keep the typed request on fixed lines so the camera never has to follow a wrapping cursor. Declare every variable before the first seek() call.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 4 stills (ask, drop, chat, outro) before writing the full film.
</start>

title: Ora 2 image model launch film
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product name, a one-line pitch, my logo, 3 to 6 screenshots of the product, 40+ images of what it creates (or photos of it), my brand colors and font, an ElevenLabs API key and voice ID, plus a royalty-free track with a clear drop (the audio file and the drop timestamp). If I skip anything, use these defaults: "Ora 2", "an image model made for taste", free images from Unsplash and Pixabay, Geist, ink #111214, the voice Samara X (19STyYD15bswVz51nqLf) on eleven_v4, and Pixabay "Cascade Breathe" (129.83 BPM, drop at 75.39s).
</inputs>

<script>
Write a 9-line voiceover in this format and adapt every line to my product:
"This is [name]. A [category]... built for [value]. [Verb] in ANY style. Give it a [input] - and it just... understands. The more you use it, the BETTER it gets. Adjust its [setting]. Its [setting]. Its [setting]. Every [output] - exactly as you pictured it. [Name]. Out now."
Use emotion tags sparingly: [softly] on the quiet lines and [excited] on the [Verb] line. Don't tag the opener, and end it with a plain full stop.
</script>

<voice>
Call the ElevenLabs API directly using my key, without an MCP. Generate 4 full-script takes in one pass and let me choose. If a line doesn't sound right, regenerate just that line 4 times and splice the best version into my take.
Shorten pauses longer than 0.28s to 0.2s, then bring each phrase 85% of the way toward the median level, adjusting gain only during pauses.
For word timings, split the read at pauses of 100ms or longer, transcribe each segment separately with Whisper, and align its first word to the measured onset. A single Whisper pass can place words up to half a second late.
</voice>

<direction>
A 22-second square launch film, 1440x1440 at 60fps, in the style of an AI lab launch: white canvas, one typeface, black ink, real images, and captions typed word by word at the exact time they're spoken.
Every control (prompt bar, settings panel, caption pill) uses liquid glass: frost the scene behind it, bend that scene along the edge like thick glass, then add a top sheen, bright rim and soft lift shadow. Glass disappears on plain white, so add a slow pastel aura in my brand colors or a blurred wash of the photo behind it.
The one emphasized word types in a gradient of my brand colors, with a faint glow behind it.
Motion rules: keep the camera drifting (push from 1.0 to 1.04 per scene; when content moves to the next scene, start at the zoom where the previous scene ended). Nothing appears instantly: use eased fades of at least 0.3s. Change images on 16th notes, with a click for each. Land scene changes on phrase starts, and align the music drop with the [Verb] line. Don't show full stops on screen.
Banned: selection-box highlights, beat-snapped slams, white flashes, 3D, templates.
</direction>

<structure>
Seven scenes, timed to the voice:

1. "This is [name]": a collage of my images drifts out as the name types in large, then gives way to the category line.
2. "made for [value]": full-screen flashes of my best images switch on 16th notes into the drop, with the line typed in white over them.
3. The drop: a glass prompt bar types a short prompt. The result card changes style every 16th note, while a black style chip rolls to each new name above a thumbnail strip.
4. "Show it a moodboard": 9 images fly into a 3x3 grid, then circle the result as "It gets you" types on screen.
5. "The more you use it, the better it gets": type two lines, with the emphasized word in the gradient.
6. The settings: show a glass panel with 3 sliders, each moving as she names it. Shift the image's hue, roll new seeds on 16ths, then turn it into a poster. Shift a blurred wash of its colors behind the glass in sync.
7. "Every [output], exactly how you see it": burst 120 of my images outward from the center behind a glass caption pill, then bring them together into my logo as the name types on. Put "Out now" underneath and hold for 2s.

Replace the prompt bar, results and sliders with my product's real input, outputs and settings.
</structure>

<sound>
Set the song so the drop lands on the [Verb] line, and anchor the beat grid there.
Duck the music under the voice with a 3-band sidechain (lows 30%, mids 85%, air 55%; 0.3s hold, 50ms look-ahead, 0.5s release). Then adjust the mids of each phrase until the voice sits about 9 dB above the music between 300 Hz and 4 kHz.
Use one downloaded Mixkit SFX per event, positioned by its measured peak: a click for each image change, a key sound for every typed letter, a soft landing on the emphasized word, whooshes, and impacts on the drop and logo. Trim each around its peak (many risers are 4 seconds). Fade the music along a dB curve under the end card. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
</sound>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t), and every caption and cut follows the word table.
2. Glass: capture the canvas behind the shape, blur it about 14px for the body, draw a lightly blurred copy magnified about 1.06x in a 12px band along the edge, then add the milk, sheen, rim and shadow.
3. Render with Playwright at 60fps using 8 motion-blur subframes, then encode with ffmpeg.
4. Before showing me anything, make a contact sheet of stills, scan frame differences for single-frame pops (only the 16th-note runs may jump), and check the voice-to-music ratio for every phrase.
</build>

<gotchas>
A [warmly] opener can sound whispered, while [excited] can feel fake. A highlight box behind a word looks like a Windows text selection. If the camera resets to 1.0 during a handoff, the zoom snaps. A 0.05s fade looks like an instant pop-in.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, write the script, send me 4 voice takes to choose from, then show me 8 stills before the full render.
</start>

title: Orange dot motion system
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a short label for the opening toggle, one hero word, a percentage for the graph, the text for the final card, one accent color, and a track with a clear beat.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 2D motion design film in 16:9. Use a warm off-white canvas, near-black backgrounds, bold typography and one vivid orange accent. The orange dot connects every scene: it starts in the UI, becomes the dot over a letter, traces a spring graph, grows into a shape and returns on the end card. A cursor makes the opening click feel real. Keep the motion sharp and controlled, with small spring overshoots and no dead time.
Banned: stock footage, gradients, glows, particle bursts, random transitions and motion that isn't connected to an element already on screen.
</direction>

<structure>
Around 15 seconds, with a visual change on every major beat.
Open: a cursor clicks the orange toggle beside "Reduce Motion". The letters bend and move into place until only "Motion" remains, with the orange dot above the "i".
Spring: the dot jumps away from the word and lands on a graph. Its path draws a spring response, overshoots the target and settles beside a "+22%" callout.
Shape: the dot shoots across a line, grows into an orange circle and fills the frame. A black rounded square rotates inside it, then stretches into a pill. The scene contracts to a single orange dot on black.
Type: words like "SPRINGS", "EASING", "KINETIC TYPE", "3D" and "SOUND" orbit the dot. The circle of type opens out into a field of tiny dots.
Reveal: the halftone field expands and flips to black, revealing the final card: "Opus 5.5", "Motion designer." and "0 keyframes".
Return: the orange dot moves back through the halftone, graph and toggle. Match the final frame to the first so the video loops cleanly.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, 1920x1080 at 60fps. Compute every visual from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Use closed-form springs for the toggle, bouncing dot and graph. Draw the graph from the same spring function that moves the dot.
3. Animate letters individually for the "Reduce Motion" to "Motion" transformation. Keep the orange dot attached to the "i" until it begins its jump.
4. Make the orange circle, rotating square and pill different states of the same shape. Preserve its position and motion through each transformation.
5. Place the orbiting words along a circular path, then move their letters outward to hand the frame over to the halftone grid.
6. Draw the halftone as a grid of dots whose sizes respond to the orange dot. Let it grow past the frame edges before revealing the end card.
7. Sync the click, dot landing, graph peak, shape changes and final title to measured beats. Render one frame per beat to check the pacing before the full export.
</build>

<gotchas>
The graph and dot must follow the same motion or the spring will feel fake. Keep the orange accent consistent across every scene. Give outgoing and incoming text separate timing so letters don't overlap. When a shape fills the screen, scale it past all four corners. Match the cursor, dot and typography in the first and last frames to avoid a loop stutter.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and four stills (toggle, graph, kinetic type, end card) before building the full video.
</start>

title: Prompt Motion site promo
text:
<inputs>
Ask me for: the gallery URL (default www.prompt-motion.com/), one entry whose prompt
gets shown on screen, and a royalty-free track around 120 BPM with a clear drop (e.g. Mixkit).
</inputs>

<direction>
A 23-second 16:9 promo for a gallery of Claude-made motion videos, built only from the site itself:
its real header, its real grid of autoplaying previews, its real entry page and prompt.
Use the site's skin: near-white page, black pills, one UI font (Geist), and Geist Mono for prompt text.
One accent (red-orange #F0442C), used only for the highlighter, the cursor halo and the dot on the URL.
One continuous camera over a single "world" layer. Never two camera moves at once.
Every clip on screen carries its creator's @handle, exactly as the site shows it.
Banned: a "Generate" button or any feature the site doesn't have, invented numbers, paraphrased
taglines, fades on everything, glass cards, gradients, bouncy type, dead holds.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 46 beats.
b0–2: frame 0 is one real reel, full-bleed. The camera pulls back until it is just the first
  card on the site's home page. The header, then the tagline's first half, land on b1.
b2–9: hold on the live page: header plus a 3-column masonry of playing previews.
b9–13: the grid scrolls, then the camera whips into one tile until it is full-bleed.
b13–16: the music drops. Three full-res reels from the gallery, one beat each, hard cuts,
  each with a dark handle chip inside the safe area.
b16–21: the last reel shrinks back into its own tile (a match cut). A cursor with an accent halo
  hovers a tile and clicks.
b21–26: that tile blooms into its entry page: the video on the left; author, title,
  Model / Stack / Posted and the prompt on the right.
b26–32: the camera pushes 1.5× into the prompt while the video slides out. A solid accent highlighter
  sweeps one phrase. The cursor presses Copy, which turns into "Copied".
b32–46: the page slides off left. The "Copied" pill lifts, relabels to the URL and docks.
  Then "Prompt Motion" and both verbatim halves of the tagline land, and a rail of real tiles
  rises on the right. The last frame is the poster: two whole tiles, both handles visible.
</structure>

<build>
1. Remotion, 1920x1080, 30 fps. Every cue lives in timeline.ts (in beats) and every string in copy.ts.
   Scenes contain no magic numbers.
2. Scrape the site first: tagline, handles, avatars, preview MP4s and full-res videos, plus one
   entry's prompt. Quote all of it verbatim.
3. Lay out the gallery once in world coordinates. Drive the camera as (focus x, focus y,
   log-scale) tracks. Tile corner radius goes to 0 as a tile reaches full-bleed, so the
   pull-back, the whip-in and the match-cut back are all exact.
4. A tile that plays before the burst uses the same full-res file with an offset startFrom,
   so the whip lands on the burst's first frame.
5. The preview MP4s don't loop cleanly, and many contain hard cuts. Run scdet on every clip.
   Loop only windows with no cut inside them, with a 12-frame dissolve at the seam, and stagger
   each tile's phase so neighbouring tiles never change on the same frame.
6. Use one cursor that homes on the live button position, because the camera keeps creeping
   during holds.
7. Conform the track to 120 BPM with its drop on the burst. Place SFX by their measured peaks.
   Fill the track's own breaks with reversed whooshes into the hits. Mix to −14 LUFS.
8. Render stills at every cut before a full render. Run QA for frozen time and one-frame snaps.
   Then have a fresh critic who didn't build it review the render, and fix what it finds.
</build>

<gotchas>
Real gallery clips carry their own HUDs, cursors and cuts. Keep overlays (handle chips, our cursor)
clear of them, and don't put a cut-heavy clip anywhere the frame should feel calm.
If the page color matches a clip's background, the tile disappears; give tiles a 1px hairline.
On a camera push, check the last frame: the header and meta rows can drift into the edge bands.
</gotchas>

title: SuperX Feature Teaser Motion Graphics

title: Claude Opus 5.5 is incredible.
text:
Claude Opus 5.5 is incredible.

I gave it a pretty simple task:

Create a Remotion-based showreel featuring my work as a developer, content creator, and open-source maintainer.

What I wanted was a cool 30-second motion graphic that introduces  me as a developer and content creator.

That was basically it.

Claude went to work for around 20 minutes, writing the Remotion code, putting together the animations, transitions, layouts, and the overall story.

And this is what it produced.

Stunning, right?!

What surprised me most is that this isn't just AI generating a few video clips.

It's AI building the video programmatically.

The entire thing is code.

Which means I can tweak the content, change the animations, swap assets, update numbers, or completely redesign a section - and render it again.

Video generation was one of those things I thought would take AI quite a while to really crack.

Turns out we're already much closer than I expected.

And for developers, tools like Remotion + coding agents open up some seriously interesting possibilities.

Interested in knowing what prompt I used?

Comment "Remotion".

title: I used Opus 5.5 to generate 50 podcast animations for extremely…
text:
I used Opus 5.5 to generate 50 podcast animations for extremely hard to visualize concepts like Jev for Legal.  Absolutely blown away. 

We're about to see an explosion of visual podcasts, this entire medium is about to shift 

Sharing my prompt below.

【作者补充制作说明】
Go through the entire [episode] cut and add full-screen animations and graphics wherever they help. Be aggressive and over-inclusive: 35–50 moments, at least 2 per chapter. The goal is to fill empty talking-head time, explain ideas, and create visual hooks.

Style. Pick an aesthetic that's genuinely interesting and very, very cool, built in JavaScript with HyperFrames and assembled in Tesseract. Inspiration (all JS, no image assets):

https://x.com/Voxyz_ai/status/2102531681450119426: paper, typewriter-tape labels, hand-drawn marks
https://x.com/donaldjewkes/status/2102801274173587569: halftone, manga and pixel print, kinetic data type

Stay inside the LegalQuants brand (read brands/legalquants/): charcoal, white and black only, Arial, and the supplied lockup top-right, static. Write a shared style bible and a component kit first, so every animation looks like the same show.

Moments I definitely want:

[LIST]

Rules

Whenever anything goes full-screen (animation, screen share or still), one of us is in a corner picture-in-picture, bottom-right, following whoever is talking.
No punch-ins or zooming on the cameras. Keep each speaker relatively centered.
Copy must be verbatim or faithful to what's said. Never invent facts, numbers or quotes.
Sync each animation's beats to the spoken words.
Keep each graphic inside one uncut stretch of audio, and leave a few seconds of faces between graphics.

Process

An Opus 5.5 agent at extra-high effort finds every timestamp where an animation could fill space and hook the viewer, with a concept for each.
Opus 5.5 at medium effort builds each animation.
Opus 5.5 at extra-high effort judges each one once on brand consistency with the others, visual interest, relevance to the narrative and creative judgment.
Only cues the judge considers egregiously bad go back for a fix. No blanket redo loops.
Assemble the full cut with PiP baked into every full-screen visual, and give me a folder of the individual animations.

title: I made a launch ad for @grouped_news in an hour with Opus 5.5 and…
text:

My part was saying what felt wrong.

title: Claude Opus 5.5 is absurdly good at 3D.
text:
Claude Opus 5.5 is absurdly good at 3D.

I reran one of my recent 3D experiments with Claude Opus 5.5.

Same prompt, same references, same real-world scene I had previously built with GPT-6 Astra.

The result was much better than I expected.

Put simply, for this specific use case, Claude Opus 5.5 was a clear win for me.

The biggest differences for me were instruction following and taste.

With the same references, Opus 5.5 got much closer to the Zelda Breath of the Wild-style look I was aiming for.

The layout felt more intentional.

It picked better camera angles.

Asset placement made more sense.

And I spent much less time fixing basic mistakes.

In my Astra version, I had to repeatedly correct things like tree roots not touching the ground, rough geometry being used where proper assets already existed, or objects being placed in ways that just looked wrong.

Opus 5.5 got much more of this right on its own.

The interesting part for me is that I have almost zero real 3D skills.

I mostly give references, look at the result, explain what feels wrong, and keep iterating.

With better instruction following and visual judgment, that loop becomes dramatically easier.

Still plenty to improve, especially indoors.

Next test is whether I can recreate the interior of the house with the same level of quality.

title: I asked Opus 5.5 to explain gravitational lensing by building an…
text:
I asked Opus 5.5 to explain gravitational lensing by building an interactive black hole lab

One prompt for the first version, then a dynamic workflow to polish it for three rounds while I slept. This is what I woke up to: 5h 28m end to end, $90 at API prices

https://blackhole.voxyz.ai

Drag the black hole and the sky behind it bends into arcs, closing into a full ring when everything lines up

Each round ran 3 agents. Two reviewers each picked 9 to 10 issues and ranked them P0, P1, P2. The third one fixed them.
Round 1: 3D materials and lighting + UI and type
Round 2: camera motion and interaction + science-communication design
Round 3: a design director deciding whether it ships + visual QA and performance

Every P0 got fixed, the rest only if worth it. When the two reviewers disagreed, it picked one and wrote down why. It backed up before each round, checked screenshots after, and rolled back anything it couldn't fix.

title: INKBOUND Pixel Runner Game Prompt
text:
Using Vanilla JavaScript, Canvas 2D and the Web Audio API, create **INKBOUND**: one self-contained HTML file in which a sumi-e ink painting comes alive as a 16-bit pixel-art runner.

A tiny ink-drop spirit races along a black brush stroke that a painter's hand paints in real time. A rival painter attacks in indigo, and the spirit survives by **jumping, sinking into the ink, absorbing small ink and stepping back**.

- No external assets, libraries, fonts, audio files or network requests. All art, text and sound are generated in code.
- The page boots into a self-playing attract demo that loops seamlessly. Any control input starts a playable run.

## 1. Rendering
- Draw everything into a `Uint8Array` of palette indices at a fixed **160x90**. Convert it to RGBA once per frame.
- Copy that frame to a full-window canvas at the **largest integer scale** that fits, centred, with black margins. Use `imageSmoothingEnabled = false` and CSS `image-rendering: pixelated`. Account for `devicePixelRatio`.
- Integer pixels only. No anti-aliasing, gradients, `shadowBlur` or rotation. Slanted lines are pixel stair-steps, and gradients are Bayer-dithered bands.
- Simulate at a fixed **60 Hz** with an accumulator, and render with `requestAnimationFrame`.
- Zero allocation in the loop: typed arrays, fixed pools and pre-built text arrays.

## 2. Palette and colour roles (29 colours; roles never borrow each other's colours)
| Role | Colours | Used only for |
|---|---|---|
| Ink | `#121110 #272523 #46423d #6d675e` | the hero, the road, the painter's ink, afterimages |
| Paper white | `#fbf8f0` | eyes, sleeve, text on seals |
| Paper / dusk sky | `#ece4d6 #e2d3bf #d9bda3 #c9a58e` | sky bands, paper |
| Mountain washes | `#bdb19a #a39a90 #857d76` | mountains, pines, speed streaks, sketch lines |
| Sun | `#f7dcae #f2c48a #e9a870` | a pale sun disc |
| Seal red | `#c8302a #8a1e1b` | the hero's scarf and every UI stamp |
| **Indigo = danger** | `#1c2a78 #3150c8 #9fb6ff` | **every** threat, warning and rival sleeve, with a light `#9fb6ff` rim on top. Nothing else is ever indigo |
| Brush / scroll rod | `#c9a24a` (band), `#efd6a0 #a8844c` (hair) | brushes and the scroll rod |
| Hands (CC0 sprite) | `#572020 #ffce96 #c2675b #ffe4ab #de9176 #f5bb8c` | hands only |

## 3. Scene
- **Sky**: dithered bands from pale paper at the top to peach dusk at the horizon (y = 44), with paper-fibre specks and a pale sun.
- **Mountains**: two parallax ridges of flat washes on 512 px repeating height strips. Each has a one-shade-darker ridge line, small wash-coloured pine silhouettes and a thin dithered mist band.
- **Speed streaks**: wash-coloured streaks whose count and length grow with speed.
- **Road**: an 8–9 px black brush stroke, top at y ≈ 46 with a gentle sine undulation (±3 px).
  - Ragged dry-brush edges and bristle streaks in `#272523`.
  - Ink drips fall from its underside.
  - It turns dry and streaky over the last 16 px before the painter's brush at x = 138, because it is being painted right now.

## 4. The hero (B `#121110`, h `#46423d`, e `#fbf8f0`)
```
RUN body (+2 alternating legs)   JUMP            CURL (apex)     SINK (only the crown shows)
...BB.......                  ....BB......    ....BB......    ...BBBBBB...
....BB......                  .....BB.....    ...BBBB.....    .BhBBeBBeBB.
....BBB.....                  ....BBBB....    ..BhBBBB....    BBBBBBBBBBBB
...BBBBB....                  ...BBBBBB...    .BhBeBBeB...
..BhBBBBB...                  ..BhBBBBBB..    .BBBBBBBB...
.BhBBeBBeB..                  ..hBBeBBeB..    .BBBBBBBB...
.BBBBBBBBB..                  ..BBBBBBBB..    ..BBBBBB....
.BBBBBBBBB..                  ...BBBBBB...    ...B..B.....
..BBBBBBB...                  ...B....B...
                              ..B......B..
```
- **Scarf**: 7–9 px of seal red streaming behind with a 2-frame flutter. It lies flat on the ink while sinking.
- **Pose registers**: bounce, lean, squash and stretch (repeat or drop one or two body rows), widening and a 1 px eye shift.
  - Ease the registers, but quantize them on a ~12 fps clock so the motion reads as hand-animated sprites.
  - Take-off, landing and each action snap to their pose instantly.
- Draw the eyes in a second pass so body pixels never overwrite them.

## 5. Hands and brushes (outside the painting: drawn on top, never collide)
Hands use "Pixel Hand Gesture Cursor Asset" by Lintnaya (CC0). They are drawn at 2x. Legend: `a #572020, b #ffce96, c #c2675b, d #ffe4ab, e #de9176, f #f5bb8c, g = e`.
```
FIST (palm21 rows 6-15)      POINTING FINGER (palm13 rows 2-15)
......aaaaaaa...             ..........a.....
.....abcbcbada..             .........ada....
....acbcbcbcea..             .........aea....
...afcecececda..             .........ada....
...aecdcdcdcea..             .......aacea....
...adecececba...             .....aacbcba....
....adbdbfgea...             ....acbceccba...
....afddbdfa....             ...afceccdbca...
.....afddfa.....             ...aecdcecbbba..
.....aaaaaa.....             ...adececcebba..
                             ....adbfbfeea...
                             ....afddbdfa....
                             .....afddfa.....
                             .....aaaaaa.....
```
- **Brush**: 4 px wide and the **same width from handle to tip**. From the tip:
  - 2 rows 2 px wide, then 2 more soaked rows (ink `#121110`, or indigo `#1c2a78` for the rival, with a light left edge)
  - 4 rows of light hair (`#efd6a0` with a `#a8844c` right edge)
  - 2 rows of gold band
  - 4 rows of black lacquer handle going into the fist
- **Painter**:
  - The fist sits at the bottom right, holding the brush straight up. The brush tip touches the underside of the road at x = 138, and the hand bobs 1 px.
  - A white robe sleeve (with a `#e2d3bf` fold, a `#a39a90` rim and a `#572020` outline) runs off the bottom edge.
  - Over a gap, the painter lifts the brush 6 px and drips.
- **Rival**: the same fist flipped vertically, brush pointing down, with an indigo sleeve (`#3150c8`, `#1c2a78` shade, `#9fb6ff` rim) running off the top edge. The eraser uses the pointing finger, flipped to point down.

## 6. Actions (play-mode controls in brackets)
- **Jump** [W / Space / ↑]:
  - Short wind-up squash (4 ticks in the demo, 2 in play), then launch at vy −3.4 with gravity 0.2.
  - Stretch on the way up, curl at the apex, and land with a squash plus an ink splash.
- **Double jump** [W again in the air]: the spirit bursts into **10 ink dots orbiting its eyes** (one dot red) for 9 ticks, hanging in place, then re-forms and relaunches at vy −3.0.
- **Sink** [S, hold]:
  - The spirit melts into the road. Use the 3-row SINK shape drawn 1 px lower, so only the crown and eyes show above the ink.
  - Ripples spread on the ink surface. It lasts at least 24 ticks, or as long as S is held.
  - Emerge with a splash on release. Sinking over a gap falls. Jumping from a sink is allowed.
- **Absorb** [D]:
  - Opens a rotating ink vortex in front of the spirit for 14 ticks in the demo, 28 in play.
  - Any small or medium arrow or flicked droplet that comes within 1.5 px is sucked in. Its indigo particles turn to ink on the way, the spirit swells and a white **ABSORB** seal with red text stamps.
  - Each absorb extends the window by 5 ticks (max 30). A miss gives a 12-tick cooldown.
  - The giant bolt, strokes and blots cannot be absorbed.
- **Back step** [A]:
  - Bursts backwards (dx starts at −3.6 and decays ×0.8 for 10 ticks, clamped at −20 px), leaving fading afterimages.
  - Holds for 24 ticks in play (18 in the demo), then drifts back at 0.45 px/tick.
- **Early-press assist**: in play, the correct move pressed up to **24 ticks early** is held and fired on that attack's ideal tick, so good players always get last-moment dodges.

## 7. Threats (all indigo)
- **Arrows**: small (9 px), medium (13 px) and a **giant bolt** (24 px, which shakes the screen as it passes). They fly in diagonally from the top right.
  - Each has a stair-stepped shaft, a head, fletching, a light top rim and a dotted trail.
  - An arrow that hits the road thunks in and quivers, then blinks out.
  - In play, a small blinking indigo "!" seal marks where an off-screen arrow will enter.
- **Flicked droplets**: 3x3 indigo drops. They are aimed from the rival's brush tip at the top right toward the spirit's head height, and splash when they hit the road.
- **Rival strokes**: the rival hand drops in at the right edge while a blinking dotted indigo guide shows the lane.
  - It then **sweeps right to left at 20 px/tick**. Its brush lays a 4–5 px indigo stroke with a light top rim, dark streaks and a splatter trail.
  - The stroke stays harmful for its burn time (capped at 19 ticks in play). Then it dries away through dithered holes over 12 ticks while the hand lifts off.
  - Lanes are screen-space lines at a height above the road that follows the ground under the hero. A stroke can have a slope and x-limits.
- **Blot**: the rival hand hangs at the top right while a drop swells on its brush tip.
  - When the target spot scrolls under it, the drop falls in 8 ticks and splats. It spreads into a puddle of radius 9 on the road (2–3 px tall, rim `#9fb6ff`).
  - It holds, then dries from 40 to 70 ticks after landing.
- **Eraser**: the pointing finger hovers while a dotted indigo outline marks a stretch of road.
  - When that spot reaches x ≈ 132, the finger rubs, growing a 60 px **gap** in the road (±3 px per tick) and scattering paper crumbs.
- The hands never hurt. Only ink on the paper does.

## 8. Attack patterns (ticks at 60 Hz; L = 0 in the demo and 32 in play)
| # | Attack | Answer | Demo script (spawn → dodge) | Length |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Medium arrow at head height | Absorb | t 20 spawn, arrive t 68+L → absorb t 64 | 110 |
| 1 | Rival flicks 4 droplets (t 20, 23, 26, 29) | Absorb | arrive ~t 64+L → absorb t 59 | 120 |
| 2 | Low stroke just above the road | Jump | t 20 warn (25+L ticks), burn 27 → jump t 46 | 115 |
| 3 | High stroke at head height | Sink | t 20 warn (25+L), burn 29 → sink t 46 for 36 | 120 |
| 4 | Blot on the road | Jump | t 10 start, spirit reaches its centre at t 70+L → jump t 59 | 130 |
| 5 | Eraser gap + medium arrow | Jump, then double jump over the arrow | t 12 start, gap reached t 58+L; arrow t 47 → jump t 52, double t 77 | 170 |
| 6 | X of two diagonal strokes centred on the spirit (arms from 22 to 2 px above the road) | Sink | warn 25+L and 29+L → sink t 44 for 44 | 125 |
| 7 | Giant bolt aimed at mid-body | Back step | t 20 spawn, arrive t 70+L → back step t 60 | 130 |
| 8 | Chapter end | – | t 0 red **END** seal + gong; t 20–49 a wooden scroll rod rolls right → left over blank paper showing **CHAPTER N** in ink with a red number and a dry-brush underline; t 50 reset the world (next chapter); t 50–79 unroll left → right | 80 |

- **Demo**: the patterns play in order 0 → 8 forever, and every dodge happens at the **last possible moment**.
- Seed every random choice from a fixed seed at each chapter reset, and reset every scroll offset, so every demo chapter is pixel-identical (one chapter ≈ 19.0 s).
- The demo starts on the unrolling scroll.

## 9. Close call, hits and judgment
- Each tick, measure the real gap between the spirit's box and each threat:
  - arrows: sample the front 60 % of the shaft and subtract a radius
  - strokes: per column
  - blot: box-to-box
- **Close call**: fires at the closest approach when the minimum gap is **≥ 0 and ≤ 4 px** (≤ 10 in play). A blot is judged only once the spirit has fully passed it.
- On a close call:
  - freeze for 5 ticks
  - for 18 ticks the whole background turns into a **pencil sketch**: region edges in `#857d76` on blank paper, light hatching on the mountains, fading out with Bayer dither
  - a red **CLOSE CALL** seal stamps above the spirit, first drawn larger for an impact frame. On the title screen, stamp it below the spirit so it never covers the title
- **An attack judged as dodged can never hurt afterwards.**
- **Hit (play)**: an arrow must reach 1 px into the spirit's box, and a stroke or blot 2 px. Falling into a gap also costs a life and bounces the spirit back up.
  - A hit costs one ink-drop life, triggers a 7-tick freeze, a shake and red sparks, then 110 ticks of blinking invulnerability.
  - In play, the giant bolt lands 3 px further ahead than in the demo, so a back step always clears it.

## 10. Play mode
- **Start**:
  - Any control rolls the scroll over the demo into "CHAPTER 1 / READY".
  - The HUD shows a red score seal, a combo "x2…x9", "BEST" with the best score, a small red seal tally (close calls + absorbs) and three ink-drop lives.
- **Chapter 1**: the fixed order. A **hint seal** above the spirit names the answer ("D ABSORB", "HOLD S", "W JUMP", "W AGAIN", "A BACK"; button names on touch devices). It appears 44 ticks before the ideal moment, turns red and blinks in the last 10 ticks, and vanishes once the right key is pressed.
- **Chapter 2+**: shuffle the 8 attacks and add one extra random attack per chapter (9, 10, … capped at 16). The same attack never comes twice in a row. Chapters are endless.
- **Pace**: speed starts at 3 px/tick and rises 0.15 per chapter (capped at 4.0). A cleared chapter refills one life (max 3).
- **Score**:
  - distance (speed × 0.05 per tick)
  - +100 × combo per close call or absorb (the combo resets on a hit)
  - +500 × level on each new chapter
- **Best score**: kept in `localStorage` inside try/catch. It is saved the moment it is beaten (every 0.5 s), when the page is hidden or closed, and at game over.
- **Game over**: "THE INK DRIED", the score, and "NEW RECORD!" if the best at the start was beaten. Press to retry; after 15 s idle, return to the demo.

## 11. Input and devices
- **Keyboard**: W/Space/↑ jump, A/← back, S/↓ sink (hold), D/→ absorb, M mute, H hides the title in the demo.
- **Embedded use (https://t.co/1pYR66UQCe iframe)**:
  - On pointerdown, call `window.focus()`, and only `preventDefault()` for touch pointers, or the iframe never gets keyboard focus.
  - Hints are per device: keyboard users always see "W JUMP · A BACK · S SINK · D ABSORB" and "PRESS SPACE TO START". Touch users see "USE THE BUTTONS / OR TAP AND SWIPE" and "TAP TO START". Switch modes on the first key or touch.
- **Touch**: draw pixel-style buttons (ink body, grey rim, turning red while pressed, labels in the same 3x5 pixel font) **in the black margins outside the game image**, so they never cover it.
  - **Portrait / tall screens**: centre the game above a row of four big buttons: BACK, SINK, ABSORB, JUMP.
  - **Landscape**: BACK and SINK on the left, ABSORB and JUMP on the right, and a small mute button.
  - If the margins are too small, drop the integer scale by one.
  - Buttons act on press (sink while held) and support multi-touch.
  - Tap = jump and swipes (down, right, left) still work in the game area.

## 12. Sound (synthesized, starts on the first input; M mutes)
- Pre-render every sound into buffers with deterministic noise.
- **Music**: exactly **19.0 s** (32 beats ≈ 101 BPM), looping in sync with the demo chapter.
  - An A-minor-pentatonic **koto melody** (Karplus-Strong plucks with DC removed), 8 bars of eighth notes.
  - A plucked bass on beats 1 and 3.
  - Taiko hits (a pitch-dropping sine plus a noise thump) and woodblock clicks.
  - A soft 16th-note shaker.
  - A breathing A2/E3/A3 drone with integer cycles per loop.
  - Note tails wrap around the loop end, so it is seamless.
- **Effects** (one per event):
  - Jump: a pluck with an upward chirp. Double jump: rising plucks and a shimmer.
  - Land: a soft thud. Sink: a downward bloop with bubbles. Emerge: a splash.
  - Back step: a whoosh. Absorb: an inhale when it opens, then a gulp and a chime.
  - Arrow: a whoosh as it enters the screen and a thunk when it sticks. Giant bolt: a heavy whoosh and a boom.
  - Droplet: a plip when flicked and a splash when it lands. Stroke: a soft "shh" warning and a sharp swish when it fires.
  - Blot: a plink when the drop falls and a splat when it lands. Eraser: a rub-rub.
  - Close call: a woodblock "tock" and a stamp thud. Chapter end: a gong, then paper rustles for the roll and the unroll.
  - Also: hit, game over and start.
- Mix through a compressor; the music sits below the effects.

## 13. Quality bar and self-check (do this before you finish)
- Crisp pixels at any size, a stable 60 fps (well under 2 ms per frame), and a silhouette you can read in the busiest frame.
- Run the demo headlessly for at least two chapters. Confirm:
  - zero collisions
  - every attack ends in a close call or an absorb
  - no console errors
  - two chapters render pixel-identical frames
- Simulate play with ideal inputs, pressing up to 24 ticks early, for 12 chapters of random order. Confirm no hits, and that doing nothing loses a life on every attack.
- With random timing, confirm no close call is ever awarded while overlapping and no hit ever follows a close call on the same attack.
- Show a screenshot of each attack's dodge.

*Hand sprites: "Pixel Hand Gesture Cursor Asset" by Lintnaya (CC0).*

title: Opus 5.5 turned one sentence into a 3D system that opens in…
text:
Opus 5.5 turned one sentence into a 3D system that opens in Blender, rigged, textured and ready to animate.

It does not render the object. It constructs it, part by part, the way a modeller would if they had a week.

> PARSE - the sentence becomes a parts list with real dimensions, nothing implied
> MASS - each part built as clean geometry, quads only, no sculpted mush
> RIG - joints and pivots placed where the object physically bends
> SKIN - materials assigned per surface, scale and roughness set separately
> PACK - exported with a named hierarchy, so a human can edit one part

Image models stop at the render. What you get is a photograph of a thing that does not exist as a thing.

That gap appears the second someone wants to move an arm, swap a material, or send it to a printer.

Rigging is what nobody automates. Without pivots you have a statue, and a statue cannot be a system.

Topology beats detail every time. A dense mesh looks stunning in a screenshot and folds the moment it deforms.

Names carry through the whole export. Every part, joint and material reads the way a person would label it.

Studios burn days on modelling and cleanup before anyone gets to the creative part of the job.

The prompt format and what each stage returns are laid out underneath.
